1. Chemometrics & Applied Statistics

Chemometrics & Applied Statistics

2. What is chemometrics?

What is chemometrics?
Chemometrics applies statistical methods to chemical data to extract meaningful information and to support the design and interpretation of chemical experiments.
IUPAC Gold Book · chemometrics · DOI 10.1351/goldbook.CT06948

3. What is this course about?

What is this course about?
AN ANALYTICAL QUESTION Three water samples are measured four times for nitrate. Which sample is clearly more contaminated, and how confident are we in that conclusion?
Nitrate measurements
SampleRep 1Rep 2Rep 3Rep 4
A · upstream2.12.42.02.3
B · tap water4.85.14.95.0
C · runoff18.519.218.919.1
  • Replicates reveal spread: a defensible conclusion needs both concentration level and variation.

1. Variables

Variables

2. Variable

Variable
In statistics, a variable is a characteristic or quantity that can take different values within a stated dataset, study, model or experiment. Its values may be observed, measured, assigned or controlled.
Introductory Statistics

3. Why do we need variables?

Why do we need variables?
  • Describe experiments through individual aspects of a system.
  • Examine aspects separately, while stating the conditions.
  • Describe relationships between these aspects.

4. Variables, values, and observations

Variables, values, and observations
Concentration and absorbance are variables. A calibration standard is the observational unit; its assigned concentration and measured absorbance are variable values recorded together as one observation.

5. Sampling locations and replicates

Sampling locations and replicates
Each measurement is one observed concentration value, while the sampling site provides the grouping context. Similar measured values do not establish an exactly uniform concentration throughout a lake.
Analyte A concentration by sampling site

6. Why do values differ?

Why do values differ?
DESIGNED VARIATION
We deliberately choose different values. |> Calibration standards: concentrations are assigned; absorbance is measured.
OBSERVED VARIATION
We measure differences rather than assign them. A variable's role depends on the study design. |> Lake samples: concentration may vary with the environment, sampling and measurement.

12. Types of variable values

Types of variable values
The value type describes the entries, not the shape of their collection.
NUMBERS
Real: concentration in mg/L Integer: replicate count Complex: impedance in ohms
2.55∈R3∈Z2+3i∈C\begin{aligned}2.55 &\in \mathbb{R}\\3 &\in \mathbb{Z}\\2+3i &\in \mathbb{C}\end{aligned}2.5532+3i​∈R∈Z∈C​\begin{aligned}2.55 &\in \mathbb{R}\\3 &\in \mathbb{Z}\\2+3i &\in \mathbb{C}\end{aligned}2.55 is a real number, illustrated by a concentration in milligrams per litre. 3 is an integer, illustrated by a replicate count. 2 plus 3 times the imaginary unit i is a complex number, illustrated by an impedance in ohms.
CATEGORIES
Sample classes: tap, lake, runoff Labels identify groups, not amounts.

BOOLEAN
Quality check: passed or failed A condition is true or false.

Its allowed truth values are true and false.

1. Mean Values

Mean Values

2. Why do we need mean values?

Why do we need mean values?
  • Summarize several values of a variable.
  • Represent many observations with one compact number.
  • Average comparable observations to reduce uncontrolled random fluctuations.

3. Example: Five dice make one experiment

Example: Five dice make one experiment

4. Example: Five dice, one sum

Example: Five dice, one sum

**Roll five fair dice and add their outcomes.** - [?] What average sum would you expect after many repetitions? - [?] Can that average be a value that one experiment cannot produce?

**Roll five fair dice and add their outcomes.** - [?] What average sum would you expect after many repetitions? - [?] Can that average be a value that one experiment cannot produce?

The expected sum is 17.5. Each realized sum is an integer, so no individual experiment produces 17.5.

set.seed(42)
dice <- sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE)
list(dice = dice, sum = sum(dice))

set.seed(42) dice <- sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE) list(dice = dice, sum = sum(dice))

set.seed(seed)
Sets the pseudorandom seed so this example can be reproduced.
sample(x, size, replace)
Draws size values from x; replace = TRUE allows repeated die faces.
sum(x)
Adds the five sampled face values to obtain one experiment sum.
list(...)
Returns the named dice and sum values together.

6. expected value

expected value
For a discrete random variable with finite expected absolute value, weight each possible value by its model probability, not by observed sample frequency.
E⁡[X]=∑x∈Sx P(X=x)\operatorname{E}[X] = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}} x\,P(X=x)E[X]=x∈S∑​xP(X=x)\operatorname{E}[X] = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{S}} x\,P(X=x)Mathematische Formel für expected value
X, E[X]
Discrete random variable and its distribution expectation.
x, S
x is one possible numerical value of X; S is the set of all possible values.
P(X=x)
Probability that X takes the value x. These model probabilities sum to 1 and weight the possible values; they are not observed sample frequencies.

7. Example: What do we expect from five dice?

Example: What do we expect from five dice?
ONE FAIR DIE
Six possible outcomes: 1 to 6 Each has probability 1/6.
E⁡[D]=1+2+3+4+5+66=3.5\begin{aligned}\operatorname{E}[D]&=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}\\&=3.5\end{aligned}E[D]​=61+2+3+4+5+6​=3.5​\begin{aligned}\operatorname{E}[D]&=\frac{1+2+3+4+5+6}{6}\\&=3.5\end{aligned}The expected value of one fair die is the sum of its six outcomes divided by six, equal to 3.5.
D, E[D]
One fair die outcome and its expected value.
1…6, 1/6
Six faces, each with probability one sixth.
FIVE FAIR DICE
Add the five outcomes. Expectations add, too.
S=D1+⋯+D5E⁡[S]=5×3.5=17.5\begin{aligned}S&=D_1+\cdots+D_5\\\operatorname{E}[S]&=5\times3.5=17.5\end{aligned}SE[S]​=D1​+⋯+D5​=5×3.5=17.5​\begin{aligned}S&=D_1+\cdots+D_5\\\operatorname{E}[S]&=5\times3.5=17.5\end{aligned}The sum S of five fair dice has expected value five times 3.5, equal to 17.5.
Dⱼ, S
Outcome of die j; S is the sum of five outcomes.
E[S], 3.5
Expected sum; each fair die has expectation 3.5.

8. Example: From a known model to measured data

Example: From a known model to measured data
THEORETICAL EXPECTATION
Fair-dice model: E[S] = 17.5. A probability-weighted, long-run average, not a required single outcome.
REAL OBSERVATIONS
Five experiment sums: 10, 13, 18, 10, 23. Finite random outcomes; each observed sum is an integer.

- [?] Why are the results different? - We can estimate the expected value from appropriately sampled real data.

- [?] Why are the results different? - We can estimate the expected value from appropriately sampled real data.

The theoretical expectation summarizes a distribution. Individual sums fluctuate and a finite sample does not have to equal 17.5. Under suitable sampling assumptions, a sample arithmetic mean estimates the model expectation; this does not validate the model from one sample.

9. arithmetic mean

arithmetic mean
xˉ=1n∑i=1nxi\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_ixˉ=n1​i=1∑n​xi​\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} x_iMathematische Formel für arithmetic mean
x̄, xᵢ
Arithmetic sample mean and observation i, in the same unit.
n, i, Σ
Sample size, observation index and sum over equally weighted numerical observations with meaningful addition. Normality is not required.

10. Example: Average five observed sums

Example: Average five observed sums
Average five observed experiment sums, not all possible outcomes. The sample result need not equal the model expectation 17.5.
xˉ=∑i=1nxin=10+13+18+10+235=745=14.8\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}{n}\\&=\frac{10+13+18+10+23}{5}\\&=\frac{74}{5}=14.8\end{aligned}xˉ​=n∑i=1n​xi​​=510+13+18+10+23​=574​=14.8​\begin{aligned}\bar{x}&=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i}{n}\\&=\frac{10+13+18+10+23}{5}\\&=\frac{74}{5}=14.8\end{aligned}The arithmetic sample mean is the sum of n observations divided by n. Substitute the five experiment sums 10, 13, 18, 10 and 23. Their sum is 74, and 74 divided by 5 equals 14.8.
x̄, xᵢ
Average and observed sum from experiment i, not individual die faces.
n, i, Σ
Five equally weighted experiments; i indexes them; Σ adds their sums.

11. Example: Average five repeated experiments

Example: Average five repeated experiments

**Repeat the five-dice experiment five times.** - [!] List the sums and calculate their arithmetic mean. - [!] Explain why a finite sample average need not equal 17.5.

**Repeat the five-dice experiment five times.** - [!] List the sums and calculate their arithmetic mean. - [!] Explain why a finite sample average need not equal 17.5.

Add the five observed sums and divide by five. The result varies across samples and is not guaranteed to be 17.5.

set.seed(42)
sums <- replicate(5, sum(sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE)))
list(sums = sums, mean = mean(sums))

set.seed(42) sums <- replicate(5, sum(sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE))) list(sums = sums, mean = mean(sums))

set.seed(seed)
Makes the pseudorandom draws reproducible.
replicate(n, expr)
Evaluates expr n times and collects each experiment sum.
sample(x, size, replace)
Draws five die faces from 1:6 with replacement.
sum(x)
Adds the five faces within one experiment.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of the five experiment sums.
list(...)
Returns the named sums and their mean together.

12. Example: Repeat the experiment more often

Example: Repeat the experiment more often

**Compare averages from 5, 50 and 50,000 independent five-dice experiments.** - [!] Change the seed and repeat. - [?] Does every larger sample have to be closer to 17.5?

**Compare averages from 5, 50 and 50,000 independent five-dice experiments.** - [!] Change the seed and repeat. - [?] Does every larger sample have to be closer to 17.5?

Under the iid fair-dice model, sample averages converge to 17.5. Finite runs need not equal 17.5 or approach it monotonically. Increasing repetitions does not repair a biased measurement or an inappropriate sampling model.

set.seed(42)
sums <- replicate(50000, sum(sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE)))
n <- c(5, 50, 50000)
data.frame(n, mean = sapply(n, function(k) mean(sums[seq_len(k)])))

set.seed(42) sums <- replicate(50000, sum(sample(1:6, 5, replace = TRUE))) n <- c(5, 50, 50000) data.frame(n, mean = sapply(n, function(k) mean(sums[seq_len(k)])))

set.seed(seed)
Fixes the pseudorandom sequence for reproducible comparisons.
replicate(n, expr)
Repeats the five-dice experiment 50,000 times.
sample(x, size, replace)
Draws five fair-die outcomes for each experiment.
sum(x)
Adds the five outcomes in each repeated experiment.
data.frame(...)
Combines the repetition counts and their calculated averages as columns.
sapply(x, function)
Applies the supplied calculation to each repetition count.
function(k)
Defines a small calculation that receives one repetition count k.
seq_len(k)
Selects the first k experiment sums without exceeding the available data.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of the selected experiment sums.
c(...)
Combines the three repetition counts into one vector.

15. Example: Does arithmetic preserve growth?

Example: Does arithmetic preserve growth?
ARITHMETIC FACTOR
Which constant factor reproduces 1600 cells from 100 in two equal periods? Apply it twice: 100 × m × m = 100m². Factor 5 predicts 2500 ≠ observed 1600. The arithmetic mean fails this growth question.
A=(2+8)/2=5100×52=2500≠100×2×8=1600\begin{aligned}A&=(2+8)/2=5\\100\times5^2&=2500\ne100\times2\times8=1600\end{aligned}A100×52​=(2+8)/2=5=2500=100×2×8=1600​\begin{aligned}A&=(2+8)/2=5\\100\times5^2&=2500\ne100\times2\times8=1600\end{aligned}The arithmetic average factor is 5. One constant factor must be applied in each of two equal periods. Applying 5 twice to 100 predicts 2500, whereas the observed factors 2 and 8 give 1600 cells. The arithmetic mean fails to preserve this growth.
A
Arithmetic average of growth factors 2 and 8: A = 5.
100, 2
Initial count 100; exponent 2 applies one factor over two equal periods.

16. geometric mean

geometric mean
G=(∏i=1nxi)1/n,xi>0G = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)^{1/n}, \qquad x_i > 0G=(i=1∏n​xi​)1/n,xi​>0G = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} x_i\right)^{1/n}, \qquad x_i > 0Mathematische Formel für geometric mean
G, xᵢ
Geometric mean and positive input i.
n, i, Π
Number of inputs, index and product over the inputs.

17. Example: Preserve the growth product

Example: Preserve the growth product
GEOMETRIC FACTOR
Same question: one constant factor for two equal periods. Apply factor 4 twice to the initial 100 cells. Predicted 1600 = observed 1600. The geometric mean preserves this growth.
G=2×8=4100×42=1600=100×2×8\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt{2\times8}=4\\100\times4^2&=1600=100\times2\times8\end{aligned}G100×42​=2×8​=4=1600=100×2×8​\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt{2\times8}=4\\100\times4^2&=1600=100\times2\times8\end{aligned}The geometric average factor is 4. Applying it in each of two equal periods predicts 1600 cells, matching the observed final count from 100 times 2 times 8.
G
Equivalent factor 4 per equal period preserves the product 2 × 8.
100, 2
Initial count 100; two equal periods lead to 1600 cells.

18. Example: Reproduce growth in R

Example: Reproduce growth in R

**Start with 100 cells and growth factors 2 and 8 over two equal periods.** - [!] Calculate the geometric factor and use it twice to reconstruct the final count.

**Start with 100 cells and growth factors 2 and 8 over two equal periods.** - [!] Calculate the geometric factor and use it twice to reconstruct the final count.

The geometric factor is 4; applying it for two periods gives 100 times 4 squared = 1600 cells.

factors <- c(2, 8)
g <- prod(factors)^(1 / length(factors))
list(geometric = g, final_cells = 100 * g^length(factors))

factors <- c(2, 8) g <- prod(factors)^(1 / length(factors)) list(geometric = g, final_cells = 100 * g^length(factors))

c(...)
Combines the two positive growth factors into a vector.
prod(x)
Multiplies the factors to obtain their total multiplier.
length(x)
Counts the factors, here the two equal-duration periods.
list(...)
Returns the geometric factor and reconstructed final count together.

20. Example: Two summaries of microbial counts

Example: Two summaries of microbial counts
ARITHMETIC: PULLED UPWARD
10, 100, 10,000 counts per 100 mL The extreme 10,000 strongly raises the mean to 3370. Not a suitable typical value for this log-scale question.
A=10+100+100003=3370\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{10+100+10000}{3}\\&=3370\end{aligned}A​=310+100+10000​=3370​\begin{aligned}A&=\frac{10+100+10000}{3}\\&=3370\end{aligned}The arithmetic mean count is 3370 per 100 millilitres.
A
Arithmetic mean of the three equally weighted counts.
10, 100, 10000
Illustrative counts per 100 mL; result has the same unit.
GEOMETRIC: LOG-SCALE CENTER
Give equal weight to logarithms of positive counts. 215.44 per 100 mL better describes this log-scale center. Keep the extreme observation; neither center establishes safety.
G=10×100×100003≈215.44\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt[3]{10\times100\times10000}\\&\approx215.44\end{aligned}G​=310×100×10000​≈215.44​\begin{aligned}G&=\sqrt[3]{10\times100\times10000}\\&\approx215.44\end{aligned}The geometric mean count is approximately 215.44 per 100 millilitres.
G, ∛
Geometric mean of three positive counts; ∛ is the cube root.
10, 100, 10000
Illustrative counts per 100 mL; result has the same unit.

21. Example: Summarize proportional changes

Example: Summarize proportional changes
ARITHMETIC: TOO HIGH FOR THIS QUESTION
Three concentration comparisons: 0.5, 2, 5 (dimensionless). 2.5 exceeds the equal-log-weight center 1.710. It does not preserve the product: 2.5³ = 15.625, not 5.

Illustrative dimensionless ratios.
GEOMETRIC: PRESERVES THE PRODUCT
The cube root of 5 matches the equal-log-weight question. G³ = 0.5 × 2 × 5 = 5. These are concentration comparisons, not successive growth periods.

22. Example: Two equal distances, two speeds

Example: Two equal distances, two speeds

A tracer travels 100 m at 10 m/s and another 100 m at 2 m/s. What is total distance divided by total time? Compare with the arithmetic average of the speeds.

A tracer travels 100 m at 10 m/s and another 100 m at 2 m/s. What is total distance divided by total time? Compare with the arithmetic average of the speeds.

Times are 10 s and 50 s. Overall speed is 200/60 = 10/3 m/s, approximately 3.33 m/s, not 6 m/s. Equal time intervals would instead give the arithmetic mean of speeds.

Example: Which average preserves travel time?
ARITHMETIC CANDIDATE
Equal-distance sections are not equal-time weights. Predicted 33.33 s ≠ actual 60 s.

At that constant speed, 200 metres would take about 33.33 seconds rather than 60 seconds.
A
Arithmetic average of the two speeds, in m/s.
t_A, 200 m
Predicted journey time if both 100 m sections were travelled at A.
GEOMETRIC CANDIDATE
A product of speeds answers a different question. Predicted 44.72 s ≠ actual 60 s.

At that constant speed, 200 metres would take about 44.72 seconds rather than 60 seconds.
G

24. harmonic mean

harmonic mean
For positive rates over equal quantities, add the corresponding times. Equal times instead imply arithmetic averaging of rates.
H=n∑i=1n1/xiH = \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} 1/x_i}H=∑i=1n​1/xi​n​H = \frac{n}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} 1/x_i}Mathematische Formel für harmonic mean
H, xᵢ
Harmonic mean and nonzero input i; rate examples use positive values.
n, Σ 1/xᵢ
n counts the inputs; add their reciprocals. For speeds in m/s, 1/xᵢ is time per metre (s/m), so H is again in m/s.

25. Example: Harmonic speed, then total time

Example: Harmonic speed, then total time
vH=21/10+1/2=103  m/s≈3.333  m/s\begin{aligned}v_H&=\frac{2}{1/10+1/2}\\&=\frac{10}{3}\;\mathrm{m/s}\\&\approx3.333\;\mathrm{m/s}\end{aligned}vH​​=1/10+1/22​=310​m/s≈3.333m/s​\begin{aligned}v_H&=\frac{2}{1/10+1/2}\\&=\frac{10}{3}\;\mathrm{m/s}\\&\approx3.333\;\mathrm{m/s}\end{aligned}For two equal 100 metre sections at positive speeds 10 and 2 metres per second, the harmonic speed is two divided by the sum of the reciprocal speeds, exactly ten thirds metres per second, approximately 3.333 metres per second.
v_H
Harmonic speed in m/s; use exact 10/3 for the next calculation.
2, 10, 2
Two equal 100 m sections; positive speeds 10 and 2 m/s.
t=dvH=20010/3=60  s\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{d}{v_H}\\&=\frac{200}{10/3}\\&=60\;\mathrm{s}\end{aligned}t​=vH​d​=10/3200​=60s​\begin{aligned}t&=\frac{d}{v_H}\\&=\frac{200}{10/3}\\&=60\;\mathrm{s}\end{aligned}The total journey time is total distance d divided by harmonic speed v H. Two 100 metre sections give 200 metres; dividing by exact ten thirds metres per second gives exactly 60 seconds. Using rounded 3.333 metres per second would give only an approximate time.
t
Total journey time in seconds, not one section time.
d, v_H
Total distance 100 + 100 = 200 m; exact speed 10/3 m/s.

26. Example: Reproduce the journey in R

Example: Reproduce the journey in R

**Travel two equal 100 m sections at 10 and 2 m/s.** - [!] Calculate section times, total time and overall speed. - [!] Check that the harmonic mean gives the same overall speed.

**Travel two equal 100 m sections at 10 and 2 m/s.** - [!] Calculate section times, total time and overall speed. - [!] Check that the harmonic mean gives the same overall speed.

Section times are 10 and 50 s; total time is 60 s. Overall speed and harmonic mean are both 10/3 m/s, approximately 3.333 m/s.

speeds <- c(10, 2)
distances <- rep(100, 2)
times <- distances / speeds
list(times_s = times, total_time_s = sum(times),
     overall_m_s = sum(distances) / sum(times),
     harmonic_m_s = 1 / mean(1 / speeds))

speeds <- c(10, 2) distances <- rep(100, 2) times <- distances / speeds list(times_s = times, total_time_s = sum(times), overall_m_s = sum(distances) / sum(times), harmonic_m_s = 1 / mean(1 / speeds))

c(...)
Combines the two section speeds into a vector.
rep(x, times)
Repeats 100 m twice to represent equal section distances.
sum(x)
Adds section distances or travel times to their journey totals.
mean(x)
Averages reciprocal speeds; taking its reciprocal gives the harmonic mean.
list(...)
Returns named times and speeds together, with units in their names.

27. Example: Pump three equal volumes

Example: Pump three equal volumes

Pump three successive 10 L batches at 10, 2 and 5 L/min. Calculate each pumping time and the overall rate as total volume divided by total time.

Pump three successive 10 L batches at 10, 2 and 5 L/min. Calculate each pumping time and the overall rate as total volume divided by total time.

Times are 1, 5 and 2 minutes. Total volume is 30 L and total time is 8 minutes, giving 3.75 L/min. The arithmetic mean 17/3 L/min instead describes equal time weighting.

rates <- c(10, 2, 5)
volumes <- rep(10, 3)
times <- volumes / rates
list(times = times,
     overall = sum(volumes) / sum(times),
     harmonic = 1 / mean(1 / rates),
     arithmetic = mean(rates))

rates <- c(10, 2, 5) volumes <- rep(10, 3) times <- volumes / rates list(times = times, overall = sum(volumes) / sum(times), harmonic = 1 / mean(1 / rates), arithmetic = mean(rates))

c(...)
Combines the three rates into a vector.
rep(x, times)
Repeats a batch volume three times, matching one batch to each rate.
sum(x)
Adds all batch volumes or all pumping times.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean, here for comparison with overall rate.
list(...)
Returns the named times and rates together.

30. median

median
Sort the sample before choosing its center.

33. Example: Find the Pb median in R

Example: Find the Pb median in R

**Use the same Pb concentrations: 0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8 and 15.0 µg/L.** - [!] Sort all five observations and calculate their median. - [?] Does a small median make the 15.0 µg/L event unimportant?

**Use the same Pb concentrations: 0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8 and 15.0 µg/L.** - [!] Sort all five observations and calculate their median. - [?] Does a small median make the 15.0 µg/L event unimportant?

Sorted Pb concentrations: 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8 and 15.0 µg/L. The middle observation and median are 0.7 µg/L. Retain and investigate the large event; neither the median nor the arithmetic mean establishes safety or compliance.

pb <- c(0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8, 15.0)
list(sorted = sort(pb), median = median(pb))

pb <- c(0.5, 0.7, 0.6, 0.8, 15.0) list(sorted = sort(pb), median = median(pb))

c(...)
Combines all five Pb concentrations into a vector, including 15.0.
sort(x)
Returns the concentrations in increasing order without discarding any.
median(x)
Returns the sample median: the middle observation here, 0.7 µg/L.
list(...)
Returns the sorted observations and median together so both are visible.

34. Choose the summary for the question

Choose the summary for the question
ARITHMETIC
Repeated measurements · peak areas · intensities · concentrations (same quantity, comparable conditions, equal weights).
GEOMETRIC
Growth factors (equal periods) · positive data spanning orders of magnitude (multiplicative / log-scale center, not range alone; convert % rates to positive factors).
HARMONIC
Speeds (equal distances) · positive quantities averaged via reciprocals (equal-time speed averages are arithmetic).
MEDIAN
Data with extreme values (middle sorted observation; less sensitive to magnitudes, but extreme events remain relevant).

35. Which summary answers the question?

Which summary answers the question?

Equal-weight nitrate replicates are 4.8, 5.0 and 5.2 mg/L. Which center summarizes the additive measurements? State your sampling assumptions.

Equal-weight nitrate replicates are 4.8, 5.0 and 5.2 mg/L. Which center summarizes the additive measurements? State your sampling assumptions.

The arithmetic mean is 5.0 mg/L for equally weighted comparable measurements. Interpretation as an estimate needs an appropriate sampling model.

Comparable, equally weighted sensors report 480, 500 and 520 µS/cm. Calculate an average. What would change if sensor precision or calibration differed?

Comparable, equally weighted sensors report 480, 500 and 520 µS/cm. Calculate an average. What would change if sensor precision or calibration differed?

The equal-weight arithmetic mean is 500 µS/cm. Different precision or calibration can require a justified weighting or correction model.

Three simultaneous phosphorus inputs are 200, 300 and 200 g/s. The question is total input to the lake. Is a mean the quantity you need?

Three simultaneous phosphorus inputs are 200, 300 and 200 g/s. The question is total input to the lake. Is a mean the quantity you need?

The total input is the sum, 700 g/s, not the average of the three inputs. A mean would answer a different question.

Microplastic counts are 100, 1000 and 10000 particles/kg. Compare an additive average, an equal-log-weight average and a median. Does this dataset alone determine the correct scientific summary?

Microplastic counts are 100, 1000 and 10000 particles/kg. Compare an additive average, an equal-log-weight average and a median. Does this dataset alone determine the correct scientific summary?

Arithmetic mean 3700 particles/kg; geometric mean and median 1000 particles/kg. The objective and sampling/scale assumptions are needed to choose a summary.

Pesticide concentrations at three sites are 0.01, 0.1 and 1.0 µg/L. Which question would justify arithmetic, geometric or median summaries? Can three numbers establish a log-normal distribution?

Pesticide concentrations at three sites are 0.01, 0.1 and 1.0 µg/L. Which question would justify arithmetic, geometric or median summaries? Can three numbers establish a log-normal distribution?

Arithmetic mean 0.37 µg/L; geometric mean and median 0.1 µg/L. Additive, equal-log-weight and middle-observation questions differ. Three values do not establish a log-normal distribution.

Three reactors in series have rate constants 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 per hour. Is being in series enough to infer a harmonic mean effective rate? What physical model is missing?

Three reactors in series have rate constants 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 per hour. Is being in series enough to infer a harmonic mean effective rate? What physical model is missing?

Series arrangement alone is insufficient. Residence times, reactor volumes, kinetics and the target quantity must be specified. Do not infer a harmonic effective reaction constant from the three constants alone.

6. Residuals Share One Exact Constraint

Residuals Share One Exact Constraint
∑i=1ndi=0\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0i=1∑n​di​=0\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0Mathematische Formel für variance
Why deviations about the arithmetic mean sum to zero

Finite observation count · Constant with respect to the index

Conditions and scope
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
  • Constant with respect to the index: c has the same value for every index i within the sum; n is a positive integer.

Starting point

Deviation from the sample mean
di=xi−xˉd_i=x_i-\bar{x}di​=xi​−xˉ
1. Sum both sides over the observations (Sum indexed equalities)

General rule

ai=bi (i=1,…,n)⟹∑i=1nai=∑i=1nbi\begin{gathered}a_i=b_i\ (i=1,\ldots,n)\\\Longrightarrow\quad\sum_{i=1}^n a_i=\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\end{gathered}ai​=bi​ (i=1,…,n)⟹i=1∑n​ai​=i=1∑n​bi​​

Add the left sides and the right sides of equalities that hold at every index. This gives a consequence; the summed equality alone does not recover every individual equality.

Application to this step

∑i=1ndi=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)i=1∑n​di​=i=1∑n​(xi​−xˉ)
  1. For each observation, dᵢ = xᵢ − x̄.
  2. Add these equalities for i = 1 through n. The result sums the left-hand residuals and the right-hand deviations.
  3. This implication needs no probability assumption. It does not say that one summed equation can recover all individual observations.

Conditions and limitations

  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
∑i=1ndi=∑i=1n(xi−xˉ)\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n(x_i-\bar x)i=1∑n​di​=i=1∑n​(xi​−xˉ)
2. Split the sum; count the same mean n times (Split a sum and count the constant)

General rule

∑i=1n(ai−c)=∑i=1nai−nc\begin{aligned}\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-c)&=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i-nc\end{aligned}i=1∑n​(ai​−c)​=i=1∑n​ai​−nc​

First distribute the sum over a difference. The second sum repeats c exactly n times and equals nc.

Application to this step

∑i=1ndi=∑i=1nxi−nxˉ\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar xi=1∑n​di​=i=1∑n​xi​−nxˉ
  1. Use aᵢ = xᵢ and c = x̄ in the general rule.
  2. Distribute the sum over subtraction. Within this observed sample, the same fitted mean is subtracted at every index. Its sum is n times x̄.
  3. The fitted mean may change between samples, but not between indices within one sample.

Conditions and limitations

  • Constant with respect to the index: c has the same value for every index i within the sum; n is a positive integer.
∑i=1ndi=∑i=1nxi−nxˉ\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i-n\bar xi=1∑n​di​=i=1∑n​xi​−nxˉ
3. Insert the definition of the arithmetic mean (Use the arithmetic mean)

General rule

nxˉ=∑i=1nxin\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_inxˉ=i=1∑n​xi​

Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.

Application to this step

∑i=1ndi=0\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0i=1∑n​di​=0
  1. The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observations divided by their count. Thus n times x̄ is exactly that same sum.
  2. Substitute this equality into the difference of sums. A quantity minus itself is zero.
  3. This is an exact property of the arithmetic mean, not merely a statement that residuals average to zero across repeated samples.

Conditions and limitations

  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
∑i=1ndi=0\sum_{i=1}^n d_i=0i=1∑n​di​=0

7. Squaring the Deviations

Squaring the Deviations

14. Repeated Sampling: Sizes 2 to 100

Repeated Sampling: Sizes 2 to 100
  • Scenario: a known illustrative normal population, μ = 10 mg/L and σ² = 5 (mg/L)².
  • Draw independent samples of sizes 2–100. How strongly do individual MSD estimates fluctuate?
  • Small samples fluctuate more. Five realizations per size cannot reliably establish bias.

15. Many Repetitions Check Average Bias

Many Repetitions Check Average Bias
  • For each selected size, simulate 5,000 independent samples and average their MSD estimates.
  • Compare with σ² = 5 (mg/L)². Monte Carlo averages approximate expectations; bias is not the fluctuation of one estimate.
  • Prepared demonstration: average 5,000 independent samples per size, then compare with the known variance.

16. Where Does the MSD Shortfall Come From?

Where Does the MSD Shortfall Come From?
Xi−Xˉ=(Xi−μ)−(Xˉ−μ)X_i-\bar X=(X_i-\mu)-(\bar X-\mu)Xi​−Xˉ=(Xi​−μ)−(Xˉ−μ)

Square, sum and collect the centered terms

1n∑i(ai−aˉ)2=1n∑i(ai−c)2−(aˉ−c)2\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(a_i-\bar a)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(a_i-c)^2\\&\quad-(\bar a-c)^2\end{aligned}n1​i∑​(ai​−aˉ)2​=n1​i∑​(ai​−c)2−(aˉ−c)2​

Center squared distances at their arithmetic mean

Expand each centered difference, distribute the finite sum, and use Σ(a_i−c) = n(ā−c). The two cross-term contributions combine with the last squared shift to leave one negative squared shift. The fitted mean removes a nonnegative term. This is an exact algebraic identity for each realization, not an expectation or an unbiasedness claim.

MSDn=1n∑i=1n(Xi−μ)2−(Xˉ−μ)2\boxed{\begin{aligned}\mathrm{MSD}_n&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}}MSDn​​=n1​i=1∑n​(Xi​−μ)2−(Xˉ−μ)2​​

Centering at the fitted arithmetic mean removes a nonnegative squared shift. The result is an exact identity, not an average statement. Open the full algebra detail for each expansion and summation operation. The population mean is ordinarily unknown; this identity explains the estimator, rather than giving a formula that requires knowing μ.

n is a positive integer, ā = (1/n)Σa_i, and c is fixed with respect to the index. The identity holds deterministically for every finite realization.

Full algebra: why fitting the mean removes a squared shift

Constant with respect to the index · Arithmetic mean of the same n values

Conditions and scope
  • Constant with respect to the index: c has the same value for every index i within the sum; n is a positive integer.
  • Arithmetic mean of the same n values: n is a positive integer, ā = (1/n)Σa_i, and c is fixed with respect to the index. The identity holds deterministically for every finite realization.

Starting point

Compare the fitted center with the population center
Xi−Xˉ=(Xi−μ)−(Xˉ−μ)X_i-\bar X=(X_i-\mu)-(\bar X-\mu)Xi​−Xˉ=(Xi​−μ)−(Xˉ−μ)
1. Square the centered difference and expand (Binomial square)

General rule

(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2(a+b)2=a2+2ab+b2

Multiplying a+b by itself gives a², the two equal cross-products ab, and b². Squaring both sides of an equality is a valid implication, not generally a reversible operation without sign information.

Application to this step

(Xi−Xˉ)2=(Xi−μ)2−2(Xi−μ)(Xˉ−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2\begin{aligned}(X_i-\bar X)^2&=(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-2(X_i-\mu)(\bar X-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=(Xi​−μ)2−2(Xi​−μ)(Xˉ−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2​
  1. Use a = Xᵢ−μ and b = −(X̄−μ) in the binomial identity. Squaring an equality gives a consequence; we do not claim to recover all signs by reversing this step.
(Xi−Xˉ)2=(Xi−μ)2−2(Xi−μ)(Xˉ−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2\begin{aligned}(X_i-\bar X)^2&=(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-2(X_i-\mu)(\bar X-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=(Xi​−μ)2−2(Xi​−μ)(Xˉ−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2​
2. Sum, divide by n and factor index-independent terms (Distribute the sum and factor the cross term)

General rule

∑i=1n(ai+cbi+q)=∑i=1nai+c∑i=1nbi+∑i=1nq\begin{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i+cb_i+q)\\=\sum_{i=1}^n a_i+c\sum_{i=1}^n b_i\\+\sum_{i=1}^n q\end{gathered}i=1∑n​(ai​+cbi​+q)=i=1∑n​ai​+ci=1∑n​bi​+i=1∑n​q​

Use linearity for each of the three summands and move the index-independent coefficient c outside the middle sum. The last sum is not simplified yet.

Application to this step

1n∑i(Xi−Xˉ)2=1n∑i(Xi−μ)2−2n(Xˉ−μ)∑i(Xi−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-\frac2n(\bar X-\mu)\sum_i(X_i-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}n1​i∑​(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=n1​i∑​(Xi​−μ)2−n2​(Xˉ−μ)i∑​(Xi​−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2​
  1. Distribute the finite sum over the three terms, then divide by the positive n. The same X̄−μ occurs at every index, so it factors out of the cross term. Its squared last term is added n times; the divisor n cancels that count. This is deterministic within each realization.

Conditions and limitations

  • Constant with respect to the index: c has the same value for every index i within the sum; n is a positive integer.
1n∑i(Xi−Xˉ)2=1n∑i(Xi−μ)2−2n(Xˉ−μ)∑i(Xi−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-\frac2n(\bar X-\mu)\sum_i(X_i-\mu)\\&\quad+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}n1​i∑​(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=n1​i∑​(Xi​−μ)2−n2​(Xˉ−μ)i∑​(Xi​−μ)+(Xˉ−μ)2​
3. Insert the sum of population-centered distances (Sum distances from a fixed center)

General rule

∑i=1n(ai−c)=n(aˉ−c)\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i-c)=n(\bar a-c)i=1∑n​(ai​−c)=n(aˉ−c)

Split the finite sum over subtraction, count c exactly n times, and substitute Σa_i = n ā. This needs the arithmetic mean of those same values and does not require probability assumptions.

Application to this step

1n∑i(Xi−Xˉ)2=1n∑i(Xi−μ)2−2(Xˉ−μ)2+(Xˉ−μ)2\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-2(\bar X-\mu)^2+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}n1​i∑​(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=n1​i∑​(Xi​−μ)2−2(Xˉ−μ)2+(Xˉ−μ)2​
  1. Σ(Xᵢ−μ) = ΣXᵢ−nμ = n(X̄−μ), because X̄ is the mean of these same observations. Substitute that sum into the cross term: −(2/n)(X̄−μ)n(X̄−μ) = −2(X̄−μ)².

Conditions and limitations

  • Arithmetic mean of the same n values: n is a positive integer, ā = (1/n)Σa_i, and c is fixed with respect to the index. The identity holds deterministically for every finite realization.
1n∑i(Xi−Xˉ)2=1n∑i(Xi−μ)2−2(Xˉ−μ)2+(Xˉ−μ)2\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-2(\bar X-\mu)^2+(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}n1​i∑​(Xi​−Xˉ)2​=n1​i∑​(Xi​−μ)2−2(Xˉ−μ)2+(Xˉ−μ)2​
4. Combine the squared shifts and identify the MSD (Center squared distances at their arithmetic mean)

General rule

1n∑i(ai−aˉ)2=1n∑i(ai−c)2−(aˉ−c)2\begin{aligned}\frac1n\sum_i(a_i-\bar a)^2&=\frac1n\sum_i(a_i-c)^2\\&\quad-(\bar a-c)^2\end{aligned}n1​i∑​(ai​−aˉ)2​=n1​i∑​(ai​−c)2−(aˉ−c)2​

Expand each centered difference, distribute the finite sum, and use Σ(a_i−c) = n(ā−c). The two cross-term contributions combine with the last squared shift to leave one negative squared shift. The fitted mean removes a nonnegative term. This is an exact algebraic identity for each realization, not an expectation or an unbiasedness claim.

Application to this step

Fitting the mean removes a nonnegative squared shift
MSDn=1n∑i=1n(Xi−μ)2−(Xˉ−μ)2\boxed{\begin{aligned}\mathrm{MSD}_n&=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i-\mu)^2\\&\quad-(\bar X-\mu)^2\end{aligned}}MSDn​​=n1​i=1∑n​(Xi​−μ)2−(Xˉ−μ)2​​
  1. The coefficients of the shared squared shift are −2 and +1, leaving −1. The left side is the defining MSD about the fitted sample mean. The result is exact for every sample. It does not by itself prove the estimator's average bias.

Conditions and limitations

  • Arithmetic mean of the same n values: n is a positive integer, ā = (1/n)Σa_i, and c is fixed with respect to the index. The identity holds deterministically for every finite realization.
Fitting the mean removes a nonnegative squared shift

17. Average the Identity over Repeated Samples

Average the Identity over Repeated Samples
E⁡[MSDn]=1n∑iE⁡[(Xi−μ)2]−E⁡[(Xˉ−μ)2]\begin{aligned}\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]&=\frac1n\sum_i\operatorname{E}[(X_i-\mu)^2]\\&\quad-\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]\end{aligned}E[MSDn​]​=n1​i∑​E[(Xi​−μ)2]−E[(Xˉ−μ)2]​

Recognize expected centered squares as variances

Var⁡(Y)=E⁡[(Y−E⁡[Y])2]\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{E}[(Y-\operatorname{E}[Y])^2]Var(Y)=E[(Y−E[Y])2]
E⁡[MSDn]=σ2−Var⁡(Xˉ)\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\sigma^2-\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)E[MSDn​]=σ2−Var(Xˉ)
Variance is an expected squared deviation

For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.

E⁡[(Xi−μ)2]=σ2E⁡[(Xˉ−μ)2]=Var⁡(Xˉ)\begin{gathered}\operatorname{E}[(X_i-\mu)^2]=\sigma^2\\\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]=\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)\end{gathered}E[(Xi​−μ)2]=σ2E[(Xˉ−μ)2]=Var(Xˉ)​

Linearity gives the displayed expectation of the finite squared-distance average; it needs no independence. Each population-centered squared observation has expectation σ². The sample mean has expectation μ under the common-mean condition, so its expected squared shift is Var(X̄). The arithmetic average of n copies of σ² is σ². The complete sample-mean argument is available with the next result.

For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.

Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.

18. The Needed Result: Variance of the Sample Mean

The Needed Result: Variance of the Sample Mean
Var⁡(Xˉ)=σ2n\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}Var(Xˉ)=nσ2​​\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}Mathematische Formel für variance
Variance of the sample mean: full derivation

Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1 · Expectations exist · Finite observation count · Common finite moments · Finite second moment · Fixed real scalars · Pairwise zero covariance

Conditions and scope
  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Expectations exist: The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
  • Common finite moments: For every i = 1 through the positive integer n, E[Y_i] = m and Var(Y_i) = v, with finite second moments. This substitution does not by itself require independence.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
  • Fixed real scalars: a, b and c are finite real constants, not random quantities; any divisor is nonzero.
  • Pairwise zero covariance: Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.

Starting point

Xˉ=1n∑i=1nXi\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_iXˉ=n1​i=1∑n​Xi​
1. Apply expectation to the mean's defining equality (Expectation preserves equality)

General rule

U=V⟹E⁡[U]=E⁡[V]U=V\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{E}[U]=\operatorname{E}[V]U=V⟹E[U]=E[V]

If integrable random quantities agree with probability one, their expectations agree. Applying E does not require independence. An equality between expectations alone does not recover equality of the random quantities, so the displayed direction is an implication.

Application to this step

Start from the definition of the random sample mean
E⁡[Xˉ]=E⁡ ⁣[1n∑i=1nXi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]E[Xˉ]=E[n1​i=1∑n​Xi​]
  1. Start from the random sample mean, a fixed-size average of the Xᵢ. Equal integrable random quantities have equal expectations. Independence is not needed for this operation.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Expectations exist: The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.
Start from the definition of the random sample mean
E⁡[Xˉ]=E⁡ ⁣[1n∑i=1nXi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]E[Xˉ]=E[n1​i=1∑n​Xi​]
2. Distribute E over the finite average (Expected value of a finite average)

General rule

E⁡ ⁣[1n∑i=1nYi]=1n∑i=1nE⁡[Yi]\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\right]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[Y_i]E[n1​i=1∑n​Yi​]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Yi​]

The sample count is fixed and positive. Move 1/n outside expectation and distribute expectation over the finite sum. This needs finite expectations, not independence. It applies to observations and also to squared deviations when their expectations exist.

Application to this step

E⁡[Xˉ]=1n∑i=1nE⁡[Xi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[X_i]E[Xˉ]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Xi​]
  1. We need E[X̄] before using the variance definition for the mean's squared error.
  2. The count n is fixed, so the expectation of the average is the average of the individual expectations.
  3. This step needs finite expectations, not independence.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
  • Expectations exist: The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.
E⁡[Xˉ]=1n∑i=1nE⁡[Xi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[X_i]E[Xˉ]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Xi​]
3. Insert the common expectation μ (Substitute common moments in a finite sum)

General rule

∑i=1nE⁡[Yi]=nm∑i=1nVar⁡(Yi)=nv\begin{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[Y_i]=nm\\\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=nv\end{gathered}i=1∑n​E[Yi​]=nmi=1∑n​Var(Yi​)=nv​

If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.

Application to this step

The sample mean is unbiased for μ
E⁡[Xˉ]=nμn=μ\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac{n\mu}{n}=\muE[Xˉ]=nnμ​=μ
  1. Identical sampling supplies E[Xᵢ] = μ at each index.
  2. The numerator is nμ, and division by n gives μ.
  3. This establishes the equality of theoretical expectations, not equality of each realized x̄ with μ.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common finite moments: For every i = 1 through the positive integer n, E[Y_i] = m and Var(Y_i) = v, with finite second moments. This substitution does not by itself require independence.
  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
The sample mean is unbiased for μ
E⁡[Xˉ]=nμn=μ\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac{n\mu}{n}=\muE[Xˉ]=nnμ​=μ
4. Use the general variance definition for the sample mean (Variance is an expected squared deviation)

General rule

Var⁡(Y)=E⁡[(Y−E⁡[Y])2]\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{E}[(Y-\operatorname{E}[Y])^2]Var(Y)=E[(Y−E[Y])2]

For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.

Application to this step

Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−E⁡[Xˉ])2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\operatorname{E}[\bar X])^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−E[Xˉ])2]
  1. After determining E[X̄], define the variance of that random mean by its expected squared deviation from E[X̄]. Finite second moments make this definition applicable.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−E⁡[Xˉ])2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\operatorname{E}[\bar X])^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−E[Xˉ])2]
5. Replace E[X̄] by the established μ (Substitute an established equality)

General rule

a=b⟹a+c=b+ca=b\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+c=b+ca=b⟹a+c=b+c

Equal values may replace one another in the same expression whenever the operations are defined. The mathematical justification of the substituted value must have been established first; substitution does not prove a statistical premise.

Application to this step

Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−μ)2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−μ)2]
  1. The preceding expectation calculation established E[X̄] = μ under common expectations. Substitute μ in the centering term. We did not estimate or observe the unknown population mean through this symbolic calculation.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Fixed real scalars: a, b and c are finite real constants, not random quantities; any divisor is nonzero.
Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−μ)2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−μ)2]
6. Evaluate variance using the mean's defining average (Use the arithmetic mean)

General rule

nxˉ=∑i=1nxin\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_inxˉ=i=1∑n​xi​

Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.

Application to this step

Now determine the variance of the fitted mean
Var⁡(Xˉ)=Var⁡ ⁣(1n∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=Var(n1​i=1∑n​Xi​)
  1. The mean is the finite sum divided by n. Substitute that definition inside Var to evaluate the variance of the sum using the previously introduced rules. The preceding centered-square expression explains why this variance is the expected squared mean error.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
Now determine the variance of the fitted mean
Var⁡(Xˉ)=Var⁡ ⁣(1n∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=Var(n1​i=1∑n​Xi​)
7. Square the scale factor 1/n (Variance under scaling)

General rule

Scaling acts quadratically on variance
Var⁡(cY)=c2Var⁡(Y)\operatorname{Var}(cY)=c^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)Var(cY)=c2Var(Y)

Variance squares the centered distance. Replacing Y by cY multiplies every centered distance by c and its square by c². Consequently variance is multiplied by c², not by c. The standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of c.

Application to this step

The scale factor is squared
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=n21​Var(i=1∑n​Xi​)
  1. The sample mean is 1/n times a finite sum.
  2. Use c = 1/n in Var(cY) = c² Var(Y). The coefficient becomes 1/n², not 1/n.
  3. The random sum stays inside Var at this step.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Fixed real scalars: a, b and c are finite real constants, not random quantities; any divisor is nonzero.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
The scale factor is squared
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=n21​Var(i=1∑n​Xi​)
8. Add variances because cross covariances are zero (Variance of a pairwise uncorrelated sum)

General rule

Zero pairwise covariances: add individual variances
Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nYi)=∑i=1nVar⁡(Yi)\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)Var(i=1∑n​Yi​)=i=1∑n​Var(Yi​)

For a finite collection with finite second moments, the variance-covariance identity includes all pairwise cross covariances. When each is zero, only the individual variances remain. Independence is sufficient for this result but pairwise zero covariance is enough.

Application to this step

Independence removes cross covariances
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2∑i=1nVar⁡(Xi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)Var(Xˉ)=n21​i=1∑n​Var(Xi​)
  1. The general variance of a sum includes pairwise covariance terms. They vanish for pairwise uncorrelated observations. Independent, identically distributed finite-variance observations are sufficient, but the weaker common-moment and zero-covariance conditions already prove this result.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Pairwise zero covariance: Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
Independence removes cross covariances
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2∑i=1nVar⁡(Xi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)Var(Xˉ)=n21​i=1∑n​Var(Xi​)
9. Insert n equal finite variances and simplify (Substitute common moments in a finite sum)

General rule

∑i=1nE⁡[Yi]=nm∑i=1nVar⁡(Yi)=nv\begin{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[Y_i]=nm\\\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=nv\end{gathered}i=1∑n​E[Yi​]=nmi=1∑n​Var(Yi​)=nv​

If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.

Application to this step

Every observation has the same variance σ²
Var⁡(Xˉ)=nσ2n2=σ2n\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}Var(Xˉ)=n2nσ2​=nσ2​
  1. Each observation has variance σ², so the sum is nσ². The squared divisor is n². Therefore Var(X̄) = nσ²/n² = σ²/n. No normality assumption is used. For correlated observations additional covariance terms would remain.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common finite moments: For every i = 1 through the positive integer n, E[Y_i] = m and Var(Y_i) = v, with finite second moments. This substitution does not by itself require independence.
  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Pairwise zero covariance: Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.
Every observation has the same variance σ²
Var⁡(Xˉ)=nσ2n2=σ2n\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}Var(Xˉ)=n2nσ2​=nσ2​

19. The MSD Is Too Small in Expectation

The MSD Is Too Small in Expectation
E⁡[MSDn]=σ2−σ2n\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\sigma^2-\frac{\sigma^2}{n}E[MSDn​]=σ2−nσ2​

Factor out the population variance

a−an=n−1naa-\frac an=\frac{n-1}{n}aa−na​=nn−1​a
E⁡[MSDn]=n−1nσ2\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2E[MSDn​]=nn−1​σ2
Factor a common value

Write a as na/n, subtract a/n and factor out a. The result holds for every real a and positive integer n. This is algebra, not an additional statistical assumption.

E⁡[MSDn]=n−1nσ2\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2E[MSDn​]=nn−1​σ2

In the general factorization use a = σ². The fraction left after subtraction is (n−1)/n, strictly less than one for n > 1. Thus the MSD is biased downward when σ² > 0. A particular realized MSD may lie above or below σ². Bias is the repeated-sampling expectation, not the direction of every individual error.

n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.

  • Insert Var(X̄) = σ²/n into E[MSDₙ] = σ² − Var(X̄), then factor the common σ².
  • The downward bias factor is (n−1)/n in expectation, not in every sample. The model assumptions of the preceding result still apply.

20. Bessel's Correction Removes the Systematic Bias

Bessel's Correction Removes the Systematic Bias
E⁡[MSDn]=n−1nσ2\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2E[MSDn​]=nn−1​σ2

Multiply by the reciprocal bias factor, for n > 1

E⁡[cY]=cE⁡[Y]\operatorname{E}[cY]=c\operatorname{E}[Y]E[cY]=cE[Y]
S2:=nn−1MSDnE⁡[S2]=σ2\begin{gathered}S^2:=\frac{n}{n-1}\mathrm{MSD}_n\\\boxed{\operatorname{E}[S^2]=\sigma^2}\end{gathered}S2:=n−1n​MSDn​E[S2]=σ2​​
Factor a fixed constant out of expectation

A constant fixed across repeated samples multiplies the expectation. A random offset such as Δ must not itself be pulled outside E; the fixed count n may be.

E⁡[S2]=nn−1E⁡[MSDn]=nn−1n−1nσ2=σ2\operatorname{E}[S^2]=\frac{n}{n-1}\operatorname{E}[\mathrm{MSD}_n]=\frac{n}{n-1}\frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2=\sigma^2E[S2]=n−1n​E[MSDn​]=n−1n​nn−1​σ2=σ2

Define the random statistic S² by multiplying MSDₙ by the fixed reciprocal n/(n−1). Linearity moves that coefficient outside E and the factors cancel. S² is unbiased under the stated assumptions. Its observed value s² is not generally exactly σ², and the square root is not automatically unbiased.

n > 1, so n−1 is positive and division by n−1 is valid.

  • Theory explains average bias. Monte Carlo means approximate the curve; they need not lie exactly on it.

24. From Variance to Standard Deviation

From Variance to Standard Deviation
sA2=133  (mg/L)2s_A^2=\frac{13}{3}\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2sA2​=313​(mg/L)2

Take the nonnegative square root

s=s2s=\sqrt{s^2}s=s2​
sA=133  mg/L≈2.082  mg/Ls_A=\sqrt{\frac{13}{3}}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.082\;\mathrm{mg/L}sA​=313​​mg/L≈2.082mg/L
Definition of standard deviation

Standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of variance. Taking the square root also restores the original physical unit. It is not the mean absolute deviation, and an unbiased variance estimate does not imply an unbiased square root.

sA=133  mg/L≈2.082  mg/Ls_A=\sqrt{\frac{13}{3}}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.082\;\mathrm{mg/L}sA​=313​​mg/L≈2.082mg/L

Series A has sample variance 13/3 (mg/L)². Take its nonnegative square root: √(13/3) ≈ 2.081666, reported here as 2.082 mg/L. The concentration unit is no longer squared. This is a root-mean-square measure of residual size with the stated divisor, not an arithmetic mean of absolute distances.

  • SD restores the measurement scale. It is not the mean absolute deviation from the sample mean.

29. What Does SD Tell Us About Precision?

What Does SD Tell Us About Precision?
  • Scenario: control sample, assigned reference 10 mg/L. Five determinations per method in one session, with fixed procedure, operator and instrument.
  • Precision is closeness of agreement among repeated measurement results under stated conditions.
  • A has smaller observed SD: closer agreement in this session, not proof of general method suitability.
Five QC repeats: values, mean and sample SD (mg/L)
MethodValuesMeanSD
A9.8, 10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.210.0000.158
B8.7, 10.8, 9.5, 11.2, 9.810.0001.007
  • Precision describes agreement under stated measurement conditions.

30. Repeatability and Measurement Conditions

Repeatability and Measurement Conditions
Repeatability
Scenario: repeat a control measurement within one short run. Same laboratory and method. Relevant conditions remain the same over a ==short interval==. Describe which operations were actually repeated.
Intermediate precision
Scenario: compare control results collected on different days. Same laboratory, with specified changes. Vary day, operator or instrument deliberately. The design determines which sources are represented.
Reproducibility
Scenario: a defined interlaboratory comparison. Different laboratories, under stated conditions. Specify the method, materials and comparison protocol. No universal quantitative ranking follows without data.
  • Choose and report the measurement conditions before interpreting an SD.

31. Precision, Trueness and Bias

Precision, Trueness and Bias
Precision
Scenario: repeat the same control measurement. Precision concerns agreement among repeated results. State the measurement conditions and independent units. Small spread does ==not establish trueness==.
Trueness
Scenario: compare an average with a suitable reference. Trueness concerns agreement of the long-run average with the reference. A small observed SD does not answer that question. Finite data only estimate the long-run behavior.
Bias
Scenario: a tightly grouped series is centered above the reference. Bias is the difference between the expected result and the reference. An observed mean difference estimates bias with uncertainty. A series can be precise and systematically shifted.

32. Why Precision Alone Is Not Enough

Why Precision Alone Is Not Enough
Scenario: same spread, different center
• Compare two series with reference 10 mg/L. • Their observed SDs agree, but their means are 10 and 11 mg/L. • Does ==precision alone== identify agreement with the reference?
Reference 10 mg/L; illustrative summaries in mg/L
SeriesMeanSD
Centered10.0000.158
Shifted11.0000.158
  • A small SD alone does not establish closeness to the reference or method suitability.

33. What Counts as an Independent Replicate?

What Counts as an Independent Replicate?
Three injections from one vial
Scenario: inject the same prepared material three times. Repeat injection and detection; vial, preparation and field sample remain shared. Instrumental variation can become visible. These technical repeats are ==not three independent field units==; drift can also correlate them.
Three independent preparations
Scenario: prepare three separate aliquots of one sample. Repeat preparation and measurement; the field sample remains shared. Preparation plus downstream variation can become visible. Independent preparation errors need justification; these are not three independent field samples.
Three independently collected field samples
Scenario: collect, prepare and measure three field samples separately. Repeat collection and downstream operations; site or time may remain shared. Field-sampling and analytical variation can both appear. Independence depends on collection design; treating nested readings as independent is pseudoreplication.
  • Measurement repetitions are not automatically independent experimental units.

34. Sources of Analytical Variation

Sources of Analytical Variation
  • An analytical result may be influenced by several sources of variability.

35. Combining Variance Contributions

Combining Variance Contributions
σtotal2=Var⁡(A+B+C)\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=\operatorname{Var}(A+B+C)σtotal2​=Var(A+B+C)

Add the independent component variances

Var⁡(A+B)=Var⁡(A)+Var⁡(B)σtotal2=∑kσk2\begin{gathered}\operatorname{Var}(A+B)=\operatorname{Var}(A)+\operatorname{Var}(B)\\\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=\sum_k\sigma_k^2\end{gathered}Var(A+B)=Var(A)+Var(B)σtotal2​=k∑​σk2​​
σtotal2=4+1+0.25=5.25  (mg/L)2\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=4+1+0.25=5.25\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2σtotal2​=4+1+0.25=5.25(mg/L)2
Variance of independent additive contributions

For independent finite-variance contributions, covariance terms vanish. Therefore Var(A+B) = Var(A)+Var(B), and the finite-sum extension gives total variance as the sum of component variances. For correlated sources Var(A+B) also contains 2 Cov(A,B). This law concerns an assumed model, not differences between pooled experimental SDs.

σtotal2=4+1+0.25=5.25  (mg/L)2\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=4+1+0.25=5.25\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2σtotal2​=4+1+0.25=5.25(mg/L)2

Treat A, B and C as additive random contributions, all expressed in mg/L. Their illustrative variances are 4, 1 and 0.25 (mg/L)². Independence removes the covariance terms. Add the three variances to obtain 5.25 (mg/L)². The numbers are model inputs for teaching, not variance components isolated from the lake or QC data.

Illustrative model, not estimated components: sampling variance 4, preparation variance 1, instrument variance 0.25 (mg/L)². Assume independent additive contributions with finite variance. Correlated sources require covariance terms.

Additive preparation contribution in the illustrative model.

Additive instrument contribution in the illustrative model.

36. From Total Variance to Total SD

From Total Variance to Total SD
σtotal2=4+1+0.25=5.25  (mg/L)2\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}^2=4+1+0.25=5.25\;(\mathrm{mg/L})^2σtotal2​=4+1+0.25=5.25(mg/L)2

Take one square root after adding

σtotal=∑kσk2\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{\sum_k\sigma_k^2}σtotal​=k∑​σk2​​
σtotal=5.25  mg/L≈2.291  mg/L\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{5.25}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.291\;\mathrm{mg/L}σtotal​=5.25​mg/L≈2.291mg/L
Take the square root of total variance

After adding variances in the same squared unit, take one nonnegative square root. Standard deviations are not directly additive. This root-sum-of-squares calculation needs the independence/additivity assumptions used in the preceding step.

σtotal=5.25  mg/L≈2.291  mg/L\sigma_{\mathrm{total}}=\sqrt{5.25}\;\mathrm{mg/L}\approx2.291\;\mathrm{mg/L}σtotal​=5.25​mg/L≈2.291mg/L

Take one square root of the total 5.25 (mg/L)², giving approximately 2.291 mg/L. Adding the individual SDs would give 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 3.5 mg/L, which is not the SD of this independent sum. If contributions were correlated, include covariance terms before taking the square root.

37. What Must We Replicate?

What Must We Replicate?
Balanced nested designs: three repetitions at each added level
Repeated levelMeasurement structureReadingsIncluded variation / shared levels
Instrumental repeats3 injections, one vial3Instrument; preparation and field sample shared
Preparation repeats3 preparations × 3 injections9Preparation + instrument; field sample shared
Field samples3 samples × 3 preparations × 3 injections27Within-site sampling + preparation + instrument; site shared
Sampling sites3 sites × 3 samples × 3 preparations × 3 injections81Between-site + all downstream variation; nested readings remain dependent
  • Each child belongs to one parent: injections within preparations, preparations within field samples, samples within sites. 81 readings are only three sites, not 81 independent sites.
  • Pooled SDs do not isolate variance components. Replication at the relevant levels plus a suitable hierarchical model may be needed to separate sources.

39. Relative Standard Deviation

Relative Standard Deviation
RSD=s∣xˉ∣,RSD(%)=100 s∣xˉ∣\mathrm{RSD}=\frac{s}{|\bar{x}|},\qquad\mathrm{RSD}(\%)=100\,\frac{s}{|\bar{x}|}RSD=∣xˉ∣s​,RSD(%)=100∣xˉ∣s​\mathrm{RSD}=\frac{s}{|\bar{x}|},\qquad\mathrm{RSD}(\%)=100\,\frac{s}{|\bar{x}|}Mathematische Formel für relative standard deviation
Spread relative to level
RSD: relative standard deviation; s: sample SD; x̄: sample mean. | | takes its absolute value. The mean must be nonzero and sufficiently far from zero.
Ratio or percentage
The units cancel. RSD is dimensionless. Multiplying by 100 expresses its numerical percentage; % denotes percent. A ratio of 0.02 is 2%.
Meaningful ratios
Use a suitable ratio-scale quantity with a meaningful zero and compatible measurement conditions. A nonzero mean alone is not sufficient.

  • SD carries the concentration unit. Convert units before comparing absolute SD values: 0.00100747 g/L = 1.00747 mg/L.
  • RSD is dimensionless (reported as %). Multiplying both the mean and SD by the same positive unit factor leaves RSD unchanged.

41. When RSD Becomes Misleading

When RSD Becomes Misleading
  • RSD is undefined at a zero mean and unstable near zero. Blank measurements need absolute-spread assessment.
  • Ratios need a meaningful zero. RSD of Celsius temperatures is inappropriate.
