43. R Practice: Evaluate Two QC Methods

R Practice: Evaluate Two QC Methods

- **Compare A/B:** means, SDs and RSDs. - **Count:** comparisons return TRUE/FALSE; sum() counts TRUE. - **Read output:** means, SDs, RSD (%) and counts; each in A/B order. - **Interpret:** [9.5, 10.5] mg/L includes endpoints and is ==illustrative, not a validated requirement==.

- **Compare A/B:** means, SDs and RSDs. - **Count:** comparisons return TRUE/FALSE; sum() counts TRUE. - **Read output:** means, SDs, RSD (%) and counts; each in A/B order. - **Interpret:** [9.5, 10.5] mg/L includes endpoints and is ==illustrative, not a validated requirement==.

a <- c(9.8, 10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.2)
b <- c(8.7, 10.8, 9.5, 11.2, 9.8)
ma <- mean(a); mb <- mean(b)
sa <- sd(a); sb <- sd(b)
ra <- 100*sa/ma; rb <- 100*sb/mb
inside_a <- a >= 9.5 & a <= 10.5
inside_b <- b >= 9.5 & b <= 10.5
na <- sum(inside_a); nb <- sum(inside_b)
c(ma, mb, sa, sb, ra, rb, na, nb)

a <- c(9.8, 10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.2) b <- c(8.7, 10.8, 9.5, 11.2, 9.8) ma <- mean(a); mb <- mean(b) sa <- sd(a); sb <- sd(b) ra <- 100*sa/ma; rb <- 100*sb/mb inside_a <- a >= 9.5 & a <= 10.5 inside_b <- b >= 9.5 & b <= 10.5 na <- sum(inside_a); nb <- sum(inside_b) c(ma, mb, sa, sb, ra, rb, na, nb)

c(...)
Combines input values or collects output results into a vector.
mean(x)
Calculates the arithmetic mean of x.
sd(x)
Calculates sample SD using the corrected variance.
sum(x)
Adds values; for logical x, counts TRUE entries.
>=, <= and &
Operators: compare to inclusive bounds; & requires both conditions.

44. Return to the Variance of the Sample Mean

Return to the Variance of the Sample Mean
Var⁡(Xˉ)=σ2n\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}Var(Xˉ)=nσ2​​\boxed{\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}}Mathematische Formel für standard error of the mean
Variance of the sample mean: full derivation

Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1 · Expectations exist · Finite observation count · Common finite moments · Finite second moment · Fixed real scalars · Pairwise zero covariance

Conditions and scope
  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Expectations exist: The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
  • Common finite moments: For every i = 1 through the positive integer n, E[Y_i] = m and Var(Y_i) = v, with finite second moments. This substitution does not by itself require independence.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
  • Fixed real scalars: a, b and c are finite real constants, not random quantities; any divisor is nonzero.
  • Pairwise zero covariance: Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.

Starting point

Xˉ=1n∑i=1nXi\bar X=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_iXˉ=n1​i=1∑n​Xi​
1. Apply expectation to the mean's defining equality (Expectation preserves equality)

General rule

U=V⟹E⁡[U]=E⁡[V]U=V\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{E}[U]=\operatorname{E}[V]U=V⟹E[U]=E[V]

If integrable random quantities agree with probability one, their expectations agree. Applying E does not require independence. An equality between expectations alone does not recover equality of the random quantities, so the displayed direction is an implication.

Application to this step

Start from the definition of the random sample mean
E⁡[Xˉ]=E⁡ ⁣[1n∑i=1nXi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]E[Xˉ]=E[n1​i=1∑n​Xi​]
  1. Start from the random sample mean, a fixed-size average of the Xᵢ. Equal integrable random quantities have equal expectations. Independence is not needed for this operation.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Expectations exist: The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.
Start from the definition of the random sample mean
E⁡[Xˉ]=E⁡ ⁣[1n∑i=1nXi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nX_i\right]E[Xˉ]=E[n1​i=1∑n​Xi​]
2. Distribute E over the finite average (Expected value of a finite average)

General rule

E⁡ ⁣[1n∑i=1nYi]=1n∑i=1nE⁡[Yi]\operatorname{E}\!\left[\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\right]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[Y_i]E[n1​i=1∑n​Yi​]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Yi​]

The sample count is fixed and positive. Move 1/n outside expectation and distribute expectation over the finite sum. This needs finite expectations, not independence. It applies to observations and also to squared deviations when their expectations exist.

Application to this step

E⁡[Xˉ]=1n∑i=1nE⁡[Xi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[X_i]E[Xˉ]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Xi​]
  1. We need E[X̄] before using the variance definition for the mean's squared error.
  2. The count n is fixed, so the expectation of the average is the average of the individual expectations.
  3. This step needs finite expectations, not independence.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
  • Expectations exist: The displayed random quantities have finite expectations. A constant moved outside E is fixed across samples.
E⁡[Xˉ]=1n∑i=1nE⁡[Xi]\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[X_i]E[Xˉ]=n1​i=1∑n​E[Xi​]
3. Insert the common expectation μ (Substitute common moments in a finite sum)

General rule

∑i=1nE⁡[Yi]=nm∑i=1nVar⁡(Yi)=nv\begin{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[Y_i]=nm\\\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=nv\end{gathered}i=1∑n​E[Yi​]=nmi=1∑n​Var(Yi​)=nv​

If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.

Application to this step

The sample mean is unbiased for μ
E⁡[Xˉ]=nμn=μ\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac{n\mu}{n}=\muE[Xˉ]=nnμ​=μ
  1. Identical sampling supplies E[Xᵢ] = μ at each index.
  2. The numerator is nμ, and division by n gives μ.
  3. This establishes the equality of theoretical expectations, not equality of each realized x̄ with μ.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common finite moments: For every i = 1 through the positive integer n, E[Y_i] = m and Var(Y_i) = v, with finite second moments. This substitution does not by itself require independence.
  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
The sample mean is unbiased for μ
E⁡[Xˉ]=nμn=μ\operatorname{E}[\bar X]=\frac{n\mu}{n}=\muE[Xˉ]=nnμ​=μ
4. Use the general variance definition for the sample mean (Variance is an expected squared deviation)

General rule

Var⁡(Y)=E⁡[(Y−E⁡[Y])2]\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\operatorname{E}[(Y-\operatorname{E}[Y])^2]Var(Y)=E[(Y−E[Y])2]

For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.

Application to this step

Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−E⁡[Xˉ])2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\operatorname{E}[\bar X])^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−E[Xˉ])2]
  1. After determining E[X̄], define the variance of that random mean by its expected squared deviation from E[X̄]. Finite second moments make this definition applicable.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−E⁡[Xˉ])2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\operatorname{E}[\bar X])^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−E[Xˉ])2]
5. Replace E[X̄] by the established μ (Substitute an established equality)

General rule

a=b⟹a+c=b+ca=b\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a+c=b+ca=b⟹a+c=b+c

Equal values may replace one another in the same expression whenever the operations are defined. The mathematical justification of the substituted value must have been established first; substitution does not prove a statistical premise.

Application to this step

Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−μ)2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−μ)2]
  1. The preceding expectation calculation established E[X̄] = μ under common expectations. Substitute μ in the centering term. We did not estimate or observe the unknown population mean through this symbolic calculation.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Fixed real scalars: a, b and c are finite real constants, not random quantities; any divisor is nonzero.
Var⁡(Xˉ)=E⁡[(Xˉ−μ)2]\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{E}[(\bar X-\mu)^2]Var(Xˉ)=E[(Xˉ−μ)2]
6. Evaluate variance using the mean's defining average (Use the arithmetic mean)

General rule

nxˉ=∑i=1nxin\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n x_inxˉ=i=1∑n​xi​

Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.

Application to this step

Now determine the variance of the fitted mean
Var⁡(Xˉ)=Var⁡ ⁣(1n∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=Var(n1​i=1∑n​Xi​)
  1. The mean is the finite sum divided by n. Substitute that definition inside Var to evaluate the variance of the sum using the previously introduced rules. The preceding centered-square expression explains why this variance is the expected squared mean error.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Finite observation count: n is a positive integer; all indexed equalities hold for i = 1, …, n.
Now determine the variance of the fitted mean
Var⁡(Xˉ)=Var⁡ ⁣(1n∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=Var(n1​i=1∑n​Xi​)
7. Square the scale factor 1/n (Variance under scaling)

General rule

Scaling acts quadratically on variance
Var⁡(cY)=c2Var⁡(Y)\operatorname{Var}(cY)=c^2\operatorname{Var}(Y)Var(cY)=c2Var(Y)

Variance squares the centered distance. Replacing Y by cY multiplies every centered distance by c and its square by c². Consequently variance is multiplied by c², not by c. The standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of c.

Application to this step

The scale factor is squared
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=n21​Var(i=1∑n​Xi​)
  1. The sample mean is 1/n times a finite sum.
  2. Use c = 1/n in Var(cY) = c² Var(Y). The coefficient becomes 1/n², not 1/n.
  3. The random sum stays inside Var at this step.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Fixed real scalars: a, b and c are finite real constants, not random quantities; any divisor is nonzero.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
The scale factor is squared
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nXi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)Var(Xˉ)=n21​Var(i=1∑n​Xi​)
8. Add variances because cross covariances are zero (Variance of a pairwise uncorrelated sum)

General rule

Zero pairwise covariances: add individual variances
Var⁡ ⁣(∑i=1nYi)=∑i=1nVar⁡(Yi)\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^nY_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)Var(i=1∑n​Yi​)=i=1∑n​Var(Yi​)

For a finite collection with finite second moments, the variance-covariance identity includes all pairwise cross covariances. When each is zero, only the individual variances remain. Independence is sufficient for this result but pairwise zero covariance is enough.

Application to this step

Independence removes cross covariances
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2∑i=1nVar⁡(Xi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)Var(Xˉ)=n21​i=1∑n​Var(Xi​)
  1. The general variance of a sum includes pairwise covariance terms. They vanish for pairwise uncorrelated observations. Independent, identically distributed finite-variance observations are sufficient, but the weaker common-moment and zero-covariance conditions already prove this result.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Pairwise zero covariance: Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.
  • Finite second moment: Y has a finite second moment, so its expectation and variance exist.
Independence removes cross covariances
Var⁡(Xˉ)=1n2∑i=1nVar⁡(Xi)\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(X_i)Var(Xˉ)=n21​i=1∑n​Var(Xi​)
9. Insert n equal finite variances and simplify (Substitute common moments in a finite sum)

General rule

∑i=1nE⁡[Yi]=nm∑i=1nVar⁡(Yi)=nv\begin{gathered}\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{E}[Y_i]=nm\\\sum_{i=1}^n\operatorname{Var}(Y_i)=nv\end{gathered}i=1∑n​E[Yi​]=nmi=1∑n​Var(Yi​)=nv​

If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.

Application to this step

Every observation has the same variance σ²
Var⁡(Xˉ)=nσ2n2=σ2n\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}Var(Xˉ)=n2nσ2​=nσ2​
  1. Each observation has variance σ², so the sum is nσ². The squared divisor is n². Therefore Var(X̄) = nσ²/n² = σ²/n. No normality assumption is used. For correlated observations additional covariance terms would remain.

Conditions and limitations

  • Common finite moments: For every i = 1 through the positive integer n, E[Y_i] = m and Var(Y_i) = v, with finite second moments. This substitution does not by itself require independence.
  • Common mean and finite variance; fixed n ≥ 1: For each i = 1, …, n, E[X_i] = μ and Var(X_i) = σ² < ∞. The positive integer n is fixed. Identical distribution is sufficient but equality of these moments is all that is needed here.
  • Pairwise zero covariance: Cov(X_i,X_j) = 0 for distinct indices. Independent finite-variance observations satisfy this condition; independence is sufficient, not necessary. Correlated observations require covariance terms.
Every observation has the same variance σ²
Var⁡(Xˉ)=nσ2n2=σ2n\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=\frac{n\sigma^2}{n^2}=\frac{\sigma^2}{n}Var(Xˉ)=n2nσ2​=nσ2​

  • **Square-root law:** at fixed population spread, four times as many independent observations halve the SE. Individual measurement spread does not shrink.

  • **Existing QC A:** 9.8, 10.0, 10.1, 9.9, 10.2 mg/L. Assuming iid repeats: n = 5, mean = 10.00 mg/L, s ≈ 0.158 mg/L.

48. What Have We Learned?

What Have We Learned?
  • A common mean can hide different observed spreads.
  • MSD describes data; sample variance estimates population variance under assumptions.
  • Fitting the mean constrains residuals, not the original sampling design.
  • SD has the original unit; RSD expresses spread relative to the mean magnitude.
  • Precision and analytical decisions require stated measurement conditions.

A report says ‘10.0 ± 0.2 mg/L’. What does ± denote? Which sample size, independent units and measurement conditions must be stated before you can interpret it?

1. Same mean. Same variance. Same distribution?

Same mean. Same variance. Same distribution?
Scenario: identical summaries
• Four synthetic sets, 100 values each. • All have the same mean and sample SD. • Do they also have the ==same distribution==?
Empirical summaries (a.u.)
SetMeanSample SD
Uniform5010
Normal-like5010
Right-skewed5010
Bimodal5010
  • **Equal mean and SD do not determine the empirical distribution.**
  • Beyond mean and SD: ECDF, quantiles and distribution shape.

2. A dataset starts with a measurement question

A dataset starts with a measurement question
Five repeated nitrate determinations of one prepared water sample; acquisition order, values in mg/L.
x1,…,xn,n=5(10.2, 9.8, 10.0, 10.0, 10.1)  mg/L\begin{gathered}x_1,\ldots,x_n,\qquad n=5\\(10.2,\ 9.8,\ 10.0,\ 10.0,\ 10.1)\;\mathrm{mg/L}\end{gathered}x1​,…,xn​,n=5(10.2, 9.8, 10.0, 10.0, 10.1)mg/L​\begin{gathered}x_1,\ldots,x_n,\qquad n=5\\(10.2,\ 9.8,\ 10.0,\ 10.0,\ 10.1)\;\mathrm{mg/L}\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für order statistic
What does i identify?
i labels the observation in acquisition order, not its rank. n counts all readings, including ties. Synthetic teaching data.
  • Repeat determinations describe this preparation, **not variability between water samples**.
  • Retain sample identity, unit and acquisition order alongside every value.

3. Parentheses turn an index into a rank

Parentheses turn an index into a rank
Sort the same five observations from smallest to largest. No measurement is removed or changed; equal values keep separate ranks.
(x1,…,x5)=(10.2,9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1)x(1)≤⋯≤x(5)(x(1),…,x(5))=(9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1,10.2)\begin{gathered}(x_1,\ldots,x_5)=(10.2,9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1)\\x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(5)}\\(x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(5)})=(9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1,10.2)\end{gathered}(x1​,…,x5​)=(10.2,9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1)x(1)​≤⋯≤x(5)​(x(1)​,…,x(5)​)=(9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1,10.2)​\begin{gathered}(x_1,\ldots,x_5)=(10.2,9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1)\\x_{(1)}\le\cdots\le x_{(5)}\\(x_{(1)},\ldots,x_{(5)})=(9.8,10.0,10.0,10.1,10.2)\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für order statistic
Same values, different meaning of the index
All values are in mg/L. x₁=10.2, but x₍₁₎=9.8 is the minimum. x₍₂₎=x₍₃₎=10.0: two observations, not one. x₍ₙ₎ is the maximum.
  • **i: observation identity. (i): rank after sorting.** Parentheses are not optional.
  • Sorted values alone cannot reveal acquisition order or a time trend.

4. Range: the span of the observations

Range: the span of the observations
For a nonempty finite sample, range is maximum minus minimum, in the original measurement unit. It describes only the extrema.
R=x(n)−x(1),n≥1R=x_{(n)}-x_{(1)},\qquad n\ge1R=x(n)​−x(1)​,n≥1R=x_{(n)}-x_{(1)},\qquad n\ge1Mathematische Formel für sample range
Order first
x₍₁₎ is the minimum; x₍ₙ₎ is the maximum. R is a width, not the endpoint pair returned by R's range(x).
  • **Only the extrema matter**, not the arrangement between them.
  • One extreme value can change it strongly. Consider sample size and context.

5. Range: repeat measurements or different samples?

Range: repeat measurements or different samples?
Two uses: different measurement questions
• Repeat: what span did 50 nitrate determinations of one preparation cover? • River: what concentrations did 50 different grab samples cover? • Synthetic teaching data; both in mg/L.
Range = maximum − minimum (mg/L)
Case (n=50)Observed span
Repeat determinations10.49 − 9.51 = 0.98
River samples25 − 0.5 = 24.5
  • Use range for the **observed span**. The river span is not repeatability; neither span is a validated working range.

6. Range: the same span can hide different data

Range: the same span can hide different data
Counterexample: two concentration profiles
• Same n=5, minimum 0 and maximum 10 mg/L. • Centre-heavy: most values near 5. • Endpoint-heavy: most values at 0 or 10. • Constructed synthetic profiles, not instrument trials.
Same range, n=5 each (mg/L)
ProfileValues → range
Centre-heavy0,5,5,5,10 → 10
Endpoint-heavy0,0,5,10,10 → 10
  • **Range misses the interior.** Compare all observations, not endpoints alone.
  • More observations offer more chances for extremes: report n when comparing spans.

7. Quartiles: three landmarks in ordered data

Quartiles: three landmarks in ordered data
The first, second and third quartiles correspond to p=0.25, 0.50 and 0.75; computed sample quartiles require the same explicitly chosen quantile convention.
Q1=Q^(0.25),Q2=Q^(0.50),Q3=Q^(0.75)Q_1=\widehat Q(0.25),\quad Q_2=\widehat Q(0.50),\quad Q_3=\widehat Q(0.75)Q1​=Q​(0.25),Q2​=Q​(0.50),Q3​=Q​(0.75)Q_1=\widehat Q(0.25),\quad Q_2=\widehat Q(0.50),\quad Q_3=\widehat Q(0.75)Mathematische Formel für quartile
Quarter, half, three quarters
Q₁, Q₂ and Q₃ are the lower quartile, sample median and upper quartile. Q̂(p) is the linearly interpolated sample quantile at cumulative proportion p. The fractions 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 are unitless; all quantile values have the measurement unit.
  • Quartiles locate positions in ordered data; they are **not distances**.
  • **Ties and interpolation:** the four parts need not contain exactly 25% each.

8. Quartiles: locate the typical concentration levels

Quartiles: locate the typical concentration levels
Two uses for nitrate summaries
• River survey: locate the middle and outer quartiles of the sampled concentrations. • Effluent: summarize central observed levels without reducing everything to the mean. • Synthetic samples, n=50 each; linear interpolation.
Q₁ / median / Q₃, linear interpolation (mg/L)
Case (n=50)Quartile landmarks
River6.625 / 12.75 / 18.875
Effluent34.5 / 59 / 83.5
  • Quartiles describe **levels**, not just widths. These synthetic summaries do not establish compliance or treatment effectiveness.

9. Quartiles: a high concentration can disappear

Quartiles: a high concentration can disappear
Counterexample: do quartiles catch a high sample?
• 50 synthetic river concentrations, 0.5 to 25 mg/L. • Replace the maximum 25 by 90 mg/L; retain the other 49 values. • Same linearly interpolated quartiles, very different maximum. • Constructed comparison, not paired field evidence.
Matching quartiles, different maxima (mg/L)
SeriesQ₁ / Q₂ / Q₃; max
River6.625 / 12.75 / 18.875; max 25
High tail6.625 / 12.75 / 18.875; max 90
  • **Always inspect the tail.** Matching quartiles neither rule out high concentrations nor justify discarding them.

10. Quantiles: choose any probability

Quantiles: choose any probability
A value calculated from observed data at probability p using a declared quantile method; it can describe the sample or estimate a population quantile under sampling assumptions.
h=1+(n−1)p,j=⌊h⌋,d=h−jQ^(p)=(1−d)x(j)+d x(j+1)n≥2,0≤p<1\begin{gathered}h=1+(n-1)p,\quad j=\lfloor h\rfloor,\quad d=h-j\\\widehat Q(p)=(1-d)x_{(j)}+d\,x_{(j+1)}\\ n\ge2,\quad 0\le p<1\end{gathered}h=1+(n−1)p,j=⌊h⌋,d=h−jQ​(p)=(1−d)x(j)​+dx(j+1)​n≥2,0≤p<1​\begin{gathered}h=1+(n-1)p,\quad j=\lfloor h\rfloor,\quad d=h-j\\\widehat Q(p)=(1-d)x_{(j)}+d\,x_{(j+1)}\\ n\ge2,\quad 0\le p<1\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für sample quantile
Interpolate between adjacent ranks
p: unitless cumulative proportion; n: number of observations; h: fractional rank; floor(h): round h down to integer j; d: unitless interpolation weight h−j. x₍ⱼ₎ and x₍ⱼ₊₁₎ are adjacent ordered values; Q̂(p) is their weighted average, in the measurement unit. The factors 1−d and d sum to one. The displayed interior case requires n≥2 and p<1; at p=1 return the maximum, and for n=1 return the sole observation.
  • The 90th percentile uses **p=0.90**, not p=90. Quartiles are special quantiles.
  • Declare the method: interpolated quantiles need not be observed values.

11. Quantiles: ask specifically about the upper tail

Quantiles: ask specifically about the upper tail
Two descriptive uses: choose p to match the question
• River: describe the upper observed concentration region with p=0.90. • Blank: summarize high blank-equivalent signals with p=0.90. • Synthetic uncensored readings; n=50 each, linear interpolation.
90th percentiles, linear interpolation (mg/L)
Case (n=50)0.9 x₍₄₅₎ + 0.1 x₍₄₆₎
River0.9 × 22.5 + 0.1 × 23 = 22.55
Blank0.9 × 0.44 + 0.1 × 0.45 = 0.441
  • The interpolated 90th percentile need not be measured. Here h=45.1: **0.9 × rank 45 + 0.1 × rank 46**.

12. Quantiles: five blanks cannot define a detection limit

Quantiles: five blanks cannot define a detection limit
Counterexample: estimate a high tail from n=5
• Compare 0,0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4 with 0,0.1,0.2,0.3,2.0 mg/L. • At p=0.95, linear interpolation puts 80% weight on the maximum. • Both are synthetic blank-equivalent series.
95th percentiles, linear interpolation (mg/L)
Blank case (n=5)0.2 x₍₄₎ + 0.8 x₍₅₎
Blank0.2 × 0.3 + 0.8 × 0.4 = 0.38
High blank0.2 × 0.3 + 0.8 × 2 = 1.66
  • A high quantile from a tiny sample is **tail-sensitive**, not a well-established population threshold.
  • A descriptive blank quantile alone is **not an analytical detection limit**; validation and error probabilities need a separate design.

13. IQR: the distance between the outer quartiles

IQR: the distance between the outer quartiles
The upper quartile minus the lower quartile, using one consistent quantile convention. The linked expression defines the descriptive sample IQR using linearly interpolated quantiles, whereas Tukey boxplot hinges may differ.
IQR(x1,…,xn)=Q^(0.75)−Q^(0.25),n≥1\mathrm{IQR}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\widehat Q(0.75)-\widehat Q(0.25),\quad n\ge1IQR(x1​,…,xn​)=Q​(0.75)−Q​(0.25),n≥1\mathrm{IQR}(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\widehat Q(0.75)-\widehat Q(0.25),\quad n\ge1Mathematische Formel für interquartile range
A width in the original unit
x₁,…,xₙ: observed values; n≥1: sample size. Q̂(p): linearly interpolated sample quantile at unitless proportion p. Subtract the lower quartile at 0.25 from the upper quartile at 0.75. IQR is this central width in the measurement unit, not the entire observed range.
  • Less sensitive to some tail changes than range or SD; **not immune**.
  • Same unit as SD, but not interchangeable with it or a confidence interval.

14. IQR: compare the central spread of recoveries

IQR: compare the central spread of recoveries
Two uses at the same fortification level
• Extraction A vs B: which has less central recovery spread? • Control series: summarize central variation over 50 runs. • Synthetic recoveries (%), n=50 each; linear interpolation.
IQR = Q₃ − Q₁ (percentage points)
Series (n=50)Central spread, linear interpolation
Extraction A102.45 − 97.55 = 4.9
Extraction B109.8 − 90.2 = 19.6
Control100.98 − 99.02 = 1.96
  • A has a smaller IQR here. For the control series, **also inspect run order**: a narrow spread does not establish stability.

15. IQR: a narrow band can still miss the target

IQR: a narrow band can still miss the target
Counterexample: same spread, shifted recovery
• Nominal control target: 100%. • Two synthetic series, n=50 each. • Medians 100% versus 110%. • Both IQRs are 1.96 percentage points.
IQR versus recovery location
SeriesIQR (pp); median (%)
Near target1.96; median 100
Shifted1.96; median 110
  • **Spread is not trueness.** Report location relative to the target as well; do not choose a method by IQR alone.

16. MAD: a median of absolute deviations

MAD: a median of absolute deviations
The median of the absolute differences between observations and their sample median; the raw statistic is not automatically scaled to estimate standard deviation.
MADraw=mediani∣xi−medianj(xj)∣\mathrm{MAD}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathrm{median}_i\left|x_i-\mathrm{median}_j(x_j)\right|MADraw​=mediani​∣xi​−medianj​(xj​)∣\mathrm{MAD}_{\mathrm{raw}}=\mathrm{median}_i\left|x_i-\mathrm{median}_j(x_j)\right|Mathematische Formel für raw median absolute deviation
Two median operations
First find the sample median; then find the median of all absolute distances to it. No squaring and no averaging of these distances.
  • R: **mad(x, constant=1)** is raw; the default scales by **1.4826**.
  • Ties can make raw MAD zero even when observations are not all equal.

17. MAD: describe typical departures, retain unusual readings

MAD: describe typical departures, retain unusual readings
Two questions for repeated nitrate determinations
• Repeat: typical departure from the median in 50 determinations. • High reading: describe central scatter while investigating one unusual result. • Synthetic series, n=50 each; raw MAD, mg/L.
Raw MAD, 50 readings per case (mg/L)
Case; median 10Median of 50 absolute distances
RepeatRaw MAD = 0.25
High readingRaw MAD = 0.26
  • Raw MAD changes only **0.25 → 0.26 mg/L** here. Retain and investigate 15 mg/L: robust does not mean unchanged.

18. MAD: zero does not mean perfect repeatability

MAD: zero does not mean perfect repeatability
Counterexample: coarse reporting creates ties
• Synthetic readings rounded to whole mg/L: 10,10,10,10,11. • Median 10; ordered absolute deviations 0,0,0,0,1. • The middle deviation is zero, but the range is 1 mg/L.
Nonconstant rounded readings (mg/L)
DescriptorResult
Raw MADmedian(0,0,0,0,1) = 0
Range11 − 10 = 1
  • Check **measurement/reporting resolution**. MAD=0 is not proof of zero underlying variation.
  • In R use **constant=1** for raw MAD; the default 1.4826 scaling cannot undo rounding.

19. SD, IQR and MAD: three different questions

SD, IQR and MAD: three different questions
Control-signal repeatability 100 synthetic normal-like readings; mean 50, sample SD 10 a.u. Same observations in each column.
Choose the question - SD: repeatability and variance-based models; sensitive to extremes. - IQR: middle-rank width for skewed data/boxplots; ignores tail magnitude. - Raw MAD: robust median distance; may be zero with ties.
Different interval choices Mean ± SD; [Q₁,Q₃]; median ± raw MAD. IQR = Q₃−Q₁ is a width, not a radius. Quartiles use linear interpolation; MAD constant 1. ==Actual closed-interval coverage, not confidence intervals or universal percentages.==

20. Same SD, different coverage: a long upper tail

Same SD, different coverage: a long upper tail
Scenario: occasional high detector responses 100 synthetic right-skewed readings. Mean 50 and sample SD 10 a.u., just as before; median 46.919.
Read the consequences - Mean ± SD: 85/100 readings, not 68. - IQR 11.024 a.u. describes the middle ranks. - Raw MAD 4.900 a.u. describes a typical median distance. - The quartile interval is not centred on the median.
Application and limit Use median/IQR or MAD when tail values dominate a mean-based summary. But retain the tail for exposure or contamination questions. ==Robust does not mean scientifically unimportant extremes may be ignored.==

21. Boxplots: construct and read the summary

Boxplots: construct and read the summary
Construction: declare the convention first
Reference: 2,4,4,5,5,6,7 mg/L. - Quartiles: use linear interpolation. - Fences: Q₁−1.5 IQR and Q₃+1.5 IQR. - Whiskers: last observed values inside. ==Whiskers end at observations, not fences.==
Reference: calculate, then draw (mg/L)
ComponentValue / span
Median line5
Box: Q₁ to Q₃4 to 5.5 (IQR 1.5)
Fences (not drawn)1.75 and 7.75
Whisker endpoints2 and 7
  • Read **median → quartile box → whiskers → flagged points**. Box length shows IQR, not SD.
  • A boxplot does **not reveal modality**, sample size or every observation. Base R Tukey hinges can differ from ggplot2 quartiles.

22. Boxplots: compare methods and sample matrices

Boxplots: compare methods and sample matrices
Two comparisons: same fortification level
50 synthetic preparations per group; recoveries (%), linearly interpolated quartiles. - Method: extraction A versus B in matrix 1. - Matrix: extraction A in matrices 1 versus 2. ==Same fortification level in both comparisons.==
Box summaries, linear interpolation, recoveries (%)
Method / matrixQ₁ / median / Q₃
A / matrix 197.55 / 100 / 102.45
B / matrix 190.2 / 100 / 109.8
A / matrix 280.6 / 90.4 / 100.2
  • Compare **median and IQR together**. The matrix-2 shift motivates investigation; these small groups do not prove a causal matrix effect.

23. Boxplots: identical boxes can hide a run-order trend

Boxplots: identical boxes can hide a run-order trend
Counterexample: keep the chronological sequence
Synthetic control-sample runs: the same five values. - Increasing: 98,99,100,101,102%. - Reordered: 100,98,102,99,101%. ==Same boxplot, different run order.== Only the first sequence is strictly increasing.
Identical box summaries, different run order
Sequence (n=5)Q₁ / median / Q₃ (%)
Increasing99 / 100 / 101
Reordered99 / 100 / 101
  • A boxplot **discards time order**. Add a run chart before judging drift or stability; five runs alone do not establish a process model.

24. Boxplots: extreme observations are separate points

Boxplots: extreme observations are separate points
==Flagged does not mean diagnosed.== Before interpreting 90 mg/L, check: - Sample identity and sampling records. - Instrument records.

25. Boxplots: a roughly symmetric central pattern

Boxplots: a roughly symmetric central pattern
==Not a normality test.== Inspect the small raw points: they reveal tail detail that the box suppresses.

26. Boxplots: a longer upper tail

Boxplots: a longer upper tail
==Large values are not automatically errors.== They may be expected tail observations. The boxplot suggests asymmetry, but does not identify its cause.

27. Boxplots: two clusters can disappear inside one box

Boxplots: two clusters can disappear inside one box
==One box can hide two modes.== - Raw points reveal the gap. - Check a histogram before calling the centre typical.

28. Boxplots: symmetry does not imply a bell shape

Boxplots: symmetry does not imply a bell shape
==Similar boxes do not imply similar distributions.== Boxplots summarize ranks. Inspect the observations and binning-based views as well.

29. R lab: build and inspect a ggplot2 boxplot

R lab: build and inspect a ggplot2 boxplot

Synthetic recoveries: **50 preparations per group**. - [!] **Run:** compare methods, then matrices. Inspect **ggplot_build()**. - [!] **Change:** the final **110 to 140**. Predict box, whisker and flag first. - [?] **Explain:** why does the box stay unchanged? ==A fence is not a whisker endpoint.== Flags do not remove observations. May download ggplot2. Local execution; no learner-data upload.

Synthetic recoveries: **50 preparations per group**. - [!] **Run:** compare methods, then matrices. Inspect **ggplot_build()**. - [!] **Change:** the final **110 to 140**. Predict box, whisker and flag first. - [?] **Explain:** why does the box stay unchanged? ==A fence is not a whisker endpoint.== Flags do not remove observations. May download ggplot2. Local execution; no learner-data upload.

50 synthetic preparations per group. Linearly interpolated Q1/median/Q3 (%): A/matrix1=97.55/100/102.45, B/matrix1=90.2/100/109.8, A/matrix2=80.6/90.4/100.2. Whiskers: 95.1–104.9, 80.4–119.6, 70.8–110; no flags initially. For A/matrix2 the upper fence is 129.6%. Changing its final 110 to 140 leaves the box unchanged, moves the upper whisker to the observed 109.2% and flags 140%; the fence is not a whisker endpoint. Synthetic grids do not establish method superiority or a causal matrix effect. Package installation requires network access; desktop R needs ggplot2 installed.

if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  if (requireNamespace("webr", quietly = TRUE)) webr::install("ggplot2")
  else stop("Install ggplot2 first: install.packages('ggplot2')")
}
library(ggplot2)
groups <- c("A / matrix 1", "B / matrix 1", "A / matrix 2")
d <- data.frame(series = rep(groups, each = 50),
  value = c(seq(95.1, by=0.2, length.out=50),
            seq(80.4, by=0.8, length.out=50),
            seq(70.8, by=0.8, length.out=50)))
d$value[150] <- 110
d$series <- factor(d$series, levels = groups)
p <- ggplot(d, aes(series, value)) +
  geom_boxplot(coef = 1.5) +
  labs(x = "Synthetic extraction / matrix", y = "Recovery (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
print(p)
ggplot_build(p)$data[[1]][c("lower", "middle", "upper", "ymin", "ymax", "outliers")]

30. Histograms: each bar represents a bin

Histograms: each bar represents a bin
Question How are 100 numerical readings distributed? Group adjacent values into equal-width bins, not unrelated categories.
Read the bars - Width: 5 a.u. per bin. - Height: observations in that interval. - A bar is not one observation or the measured signal height.
Check the boundaries Intervals are [left,right); the last includes its right edge. ==Every observation is counted exactly once.==

31. Read a histogram: centre, spread and occupancy

Read a histogram: centre, spread and occupancy
Limit ==Taller means more observations in this interval==, not higher concentration or proof of a population distribution.

32. Read a histogram: a long right tail

Read a histogram: a long right tail
Investigate, do not diagnose Sampling, mixtures or contamination may matter. ==A tail value is not automatically an error.== Time order is absent.

33. Read a histogram: two occupied regions

Read a histogram: two occupied regions
Next question Check matrix, batch or method labels. The plot suggests subgroups; it does not identify their cause or significance.

34. 2D histograms: bin paired measurements on two axes

2D histograms: bin paired measurements on two axes
Scenario: paired measurements 60 concentration/response pairs. Keep each pair together and count observations in rectangular cells.
Read a cell - Intersection of an x bin and a y bin. - Number and color encode count. - Empty cell: zero observations.
Do not confuse the encodings Equal widths within each axis. ==Color is frequency, not response magnitude.== Read both axes and the count scale.

35. Read a 2D histogram: an upward band, not a calibration

Read a 2D histogram: an upward band, not a calibration
Limit Binning hides exact pairs and within-cell scatter. ==Not a fitted calibration==, proof of linearity or a causal conclusion.

36. Bin width too large: the structure is averaged away

Bin width too large: the structure is averaged away
Verdict for this question ==Too coarse.== A correct count can still be an unhelpful view.

37. Bin width too small: occupancy becomes fragmented

Bin width too small: occupancy becomes fragmented
Verdict for this question Too little aggregation. ==More bins is not automatically more information.==

38. A useful resolution: compare the same data again

A useful resolution: compare the same data again
Still check alternatives Useful here, not universally optimal. Compare neighboring widths and the instrument's resolution.

39. Bin origin matters as well as width

Bin origin matters as well as width
One change Width stays 4 a.u.; move the first edge 30 → 32. All 100 responses remain covered.
Watch the boundaries Some observations enter different bins and heights change. ==No measured value changed.==
Comparison rule Trust features that survive reasonable changes. Compare groups with common edges and compatible normalization.

40. Bin rules are starting points

Bin rules are starting points
Freedman–Diaconis (FD) uses IQR, Scott's rule uses SD, and Sturges' rule suggests a bin count.
hFD=2 IQR n−1/3hScott=3.5 s n−1/3kSturges=⌈1+log⁡2n⌉\begin{gathered}h_{FD}=2\,\mathrm{IQR}\,n^{-1/3}\\h_{Scott}=3.5\,s\,n^{-1/3}\\k_{Sturges}=\lceil1+\log_2 n\rceil\end{gathered}hFD​=2IQRn−1/3hScott​=3.5sn−1/3kSturges​=⌈1+log2​n⌉​\begin{gathered}h_{FD}=2\,\mathrm{IQR}\,n^{-1/3}\\h_{Scott}=3.5\,s\,n^{-1/3}\\k_{Sturges}=\lceil1+\log_2 n\rceil\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für histogram bin width
Names and symbols
FD = Freedman–Diaconis; Scott = Scott's rule; Sturges = Sturges' rule. h: width; k: bin count; n: observations; s: sample SD. IQR uses linear interpolation.
  • For h>0 start with **ceil((max−min)/h)** bins; convenient-edge rounding can change that count.
  • **IQR=0 gives FD width 0.** Handle ties/constant data explicitly; no rule is universally best.

41. Apply a rule, then inspect neighboring choices

Apply a rule, then inspect neighboring choices
Explore the same 100 readings Sample SD 10, linearly interpolated IQR 13.35, observed span 51.59 a.u. Change width and origin on the right.
Starting rules - Freedman–Diaconis: width ≈5.75. - Scott: width ≈7.54. - Sturges: 8 bins over the observed span.
Try it Choose a rule, move the sliders, then Reset bins. The covering grid may add a boundary bin. ==The count must stay 100.==

42. Unequal bins: compare areas

Unequal bins: compare areas
Equal widths are optional. Adaptive bins can be narrow in dense regions and wide in sparse tails.
hj=bj+1−bjdj=njn hjdjhj=njn,∑jdjhj=1\begin{gathered}h_j=b_{j+1}-b_j\\d_j=\frac{n_j}{n\,h_j}\\d_jh_j=\frac{n_j}{n},\qquad\sum_j d_jh_j=1\end{gathered}hj​=bj+1​−bj​dj​=nhj​nj​​dj​hj​=nnj​​,j∑​dj​hj​=1​\begin{gathered}h_j=b_{j+1}-b_j\\d_j=\frac{n_j}{n\,h_j}\\d_jh_j=\frac{n_j}{n},\qquad\sum_j d_jh_j=1\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für histogram density
Reading the symbols
b: edges; hⱼ: bin width; nⱼ: count; n: total. Density has inverse measurement units; bar area is the sample fraction.
  • Raw count heights would visually reward wide bins. Use **count / (n × bin width)** for relative-frequency density.
  • The area of each bar is its sample fraction; total area is **1**. Density can exceed 1 without representing a probability above 100%.

43. Unequal bins, step 1: sort and choose ranks

Unequal bins, step 1: sort and choose ranks
Small calculation, not an application-sized dataset Eight constructed concentrations: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20 mg/L. We want four bins following the occupied ranks, rather than equal measurement widths. - Choose boundaries at minimum, Q₁, median, Q₃, maximum. - For linear interpolation, h = 1 + (n−1)p. Here n = 8. - Interpolate between the observations at ranks floor(h) and floor(h)+1. ==This is one data-dependent choice, not a unique correct partition.==

44. Step 2: calculate the actual edges

Step 2: calculate the actual edges
Use n = 8 and x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 20 - p = .25: h = 2.75 → Q₁ = 2 + .75(3−2) = 2.75. - p = .50: h = 4.5 → median = 4 + .5(5−4) = 4.5. - p = .75: h = 6.25 → Q₃ = 6 + .25(10−6) = 7. Edges: 1, 2.75, 4.5, 7, 20 mg/L. Widths: 1.75, 1.75, 2.5, 13 mg/L. Count once: [1,2.75), [2.75,4.5), [4.5,7), [7,20]. Each contains two observations. With ties, equal counts are not guaranteed; merge repeated boundaries.

45. Step 3: heights must preserve area

Step 3: heights must preserve area
Same count, unequal width Each bin contains 2/8 = 25% of the observations. Density height = count / (n × width). - First two bins: .25/1.75 = 1/7 ≈ .14286. - Third: .25/2.5 = .10. - Last: .25/13 = 1/52 ≈ .01923 (mg/L)⁻¹. ==Height × width = .25 for every bar; total area = 1.== The tall first bar does not contain more observations than the wide last bar.

46. Construct adaptive bins with quantile boundaries

Construct adaptive bins with quantile boundaries
Return to 100 readings After the worked construction, use min, linearly interpolated Q₁, median, Q₃ and max as adaptive boundaries.
Edges and occupancy - Edges ≈39.93, 42.84, 46.92, 53.86, 93.69. - 25 observations per bin. - Different widths, different heights.
Area check ==Each area is 25%.== Height is 0.25/width. Merge repeated quantile edges instead of creating zero-width bins.

47. Adaptive bins: resolve the bulk without overstating the tail

Adaptive bins: resolve the bulk without overstating the tail
Application Resolve a dense low-response region while summarizing a sparse long upper tail.
Benefit - Narrow bins near the bulk. - Fewer almost-empty tail bins. - The low last bar still has 25% area.
Trade-off Wide bins hide tail detail. Disclose edges; use common edges for comparisons. Adaptive means data-dependent, not changing per observation.

48. R lab: change bin width, not the observations

R lab: change bin width, not the observations

Same **100 synthetic two-cluster responses**; only binning changes. - [!] **Run:** read both axes; inspect bin counts. - [!] **Change:** set **bin_width from 4 to 40**. Run again. - [?] **Explain:** which structure disappears without changing observations? ==Check: all bin counts still sum to 100.== May download ggplot2. Local execution; no learner-data upload.

Same **100 synthetic two-cluster responses**; only binning changes. - [!] **Run:** read both axes; inspect bin counts. - [!] **Change:** set **bin_width from 4 to 40**. Run again. - [?] **Explain:** which structure disappears without changing observations? ==Check: all bin counts still sum to 100.== May download ggplot2. Local execution; no learner-data upload.

At width 4 the plot has 10 bins spanning 30–70 a.u. and shows two occupied regions; total count is 100. At width 40 one bin contains all 100 observations and hides the gap. No observation was changed or lost. For unequal widths, map y=after_stat(density) and supply explicit breaks; then bar area, not raw count height, represents relative frequency.

49. A bin-free view of the frequency distribution?

A bin-free view of the frequency distribution?
Same data, different histograms Bin width and origin change the picture, not the data. We want an empirical distribution view without those choices. - Parameter-free counting: no bins, bandwidth or assumed distribution family. - Cumulative: at each value, report the fraction at or below it. - Objective for the same data: no subjective bin selection; sampling bias and measurement limits remain. ==The ECDF accumulates frequencies. It is not a density curve.==

50. ECDF: one cumulative count for every threshold

ECDF: one cumulative count for every threshold
Empirical cumulative distribution function For each x, count every observation with xᵢ ≤ x and divide by n. The indicator in the formula is 1 when the condition holds, otherwise 0. - Sort the data, retaining identities and ties. - At each observed value, add its multiplicity/n. - Hold the fraction constant until the next value. ==No bins, no fitted population model.== Below the minimum the ECDF is 0; at and above the maximum it is 1. It includes the jump at x: right-continuity.
Fn(x)=1n∑i=1n1{xi≤x}F_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{x_i\le x\}Fn​(x)=n1​i=1∑n​1{xi​≤x}F_n(x)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}\{x_i\le x\}Mathematische Formel für empirical cumulative distribution function
Fₙ(x) and x
Fₙ(x): unitless sample fraction at or below threshold x. The threshold x has the measurement unit.
xᵢ, n, i and Σ
xᵢ: observed value i; n: sample size; i: index 1 to n; Σ: sum over every observation, including ties.
1{xᵢ ≤ x}
Indicator: 1 when xᵢ ≤ x, otherwise 0. Equality is included: tied values enter together. Dividing the count by n gives the fraction.

51. Calculate an ECDF: include every tie

Calculate an ECDF: include every tie
Seven-value hand calculation Sorted synthetic concentrations: 2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7 mg/L. - At x = 3.9: 1 value included → 1/7. - At x = 4: both tied 4s enter → 3/7. - At x = 4.1: no new value → still 3/7. The jump at 4 is 2/7, not 1/7. Filled endpoints are included; open endpoints are left limits. The vertical connector is not a set of intermediate function values.

52. Answer the river question exactly

Answer the river question exactly
Scenario 50 constructed river concentrations: 0.5, 1.0, …, 25.0 mg/L. Not environmental evidence. Interpretation At 12.3 mg/L, 24 observations are included: 24/50 = 48%. There are no observations between 12 and 12.5, so this segment is flat. At 12.5: 25/50 = 50%. For an interval (a,b], subtract Fₙ(a) from Fₙ(b). This is an observed sample fraction, not an estimate with guaranteed precision or a regulatory conclusion.

53. Different shapes, identical mean and SD

Different shapes, identical mean and SD
Scenario: four synthetic detector series 100 observations each; all have mean 50, sample SD 10 a.u. Interpretation - Uniform: nearly steady rise across its range. - Normal-like: faster rise near the centre, slower in the tails. - Right-skewed: rapid early rise, then a long upper tail. - Bimodal: two rising regions separated by a plateau. Steep regions mean many observations in a short interval; a plateau means none in that interval. An ECDF is not a density curve.

54. Crossing curves: which series is higher depends on x

Crossing curves: which series is higher depends on x
Scenario: compare response distributions Focus on the uniform and normal-like series, each n = 100. Compare the curves below and above 50 a.u. Interpretation Their curves cross: one can include a larger fraction at a low threshold and a smaller fraction at a higher threshold. ==No single mean or universal ranking answers every threshold question.== A higher ECDF at x means more values ≤ x, not larger measurement values. This descriptive comparison is not a significance test or proof that one analytical method is better.

55. Read backwards: inverse ECDF versus linear interpolation

Read backwards: inverse ECDF versus linear interpolation
Scenario: the same 50 river samples Ask for the smallest observed x with Fₙ(x) ≥ .25. It is observation ceil(50 × .25) = rank 13, hence 6.5 mg/L. Interpretation The generalized inverse selects an observed value. Linear interpolation instead uses h = 1 + 49 × .25 = 13.25, between 6.5 and 7: 6.625 mg/L. ==Both conventions are explicit, but they are not identical.== At p = 0, software conventions need separate care; the generalized inverse here is defined for 0 < p ≤ 1.

56. First moment: the mean locates the data

First moment: the mean locates the data
Meaning The arithmetic mean is the first raw moment: the balancing point of equally weighted observations. It uses the measurement unit. Compare three shapes 100 synthetic values each: uniform, normal-like and strongly right-skewed. All have mean 50 a.u., despite different shapes. The next 3×3 panel shows the same series as points, a boxplot and a histogram. A cyan line marks the mean in every subplot. Limit: the mean need not be a typical observation and is sensitive to extremes. It does not reveal spread or shape.
μ=E⁡[X]xˉ=1n∑i=1nxi\begin{gathered}\mu=\operatorname{E}[X]\\\bar{x}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\end{gathered}μ=E[X]xˉ=n1​i=1∑n​xi​​\begin{gathered}\mu=\operatorname{E}[X]\\\bar{x}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für arithmetic mean
X, xᵢ, i and n
X: random measurement variable; xᵢ: observed value i; i: index 1 to n; n: sample size.
μ and x̄
μ: population mean; x̄: mean of this sample. Both use the measurement unit; an observed x̄ need not equal μ.
E[ ], Σ and 1/n
E[ ]: probability-weighted population expectation, requiring a finite first absolute moment. Σ adds observations i = 1 to n; 1/n forms their empirical average.

57. Mean: one centre, three distributions and three views

Mean: one centre, three distributions and three views

58. Second central moment: variance measures squared spread

Second central moment: variance measures squared spread
Meaning Centre each value on the mean, square the deviation, then average. The result has squared measurement units and is unchanged by an additive offset. Keep conventions explicit Descriptive variance m₂ uses n. Sample variance s² uses n−1. For our 100-reading series, m₂ = 99 a.u.² and s² = 100 a.u.². The next panels shade mean ± √m₂, a scale guide in a.u., not variance itself or a fixed-coverage interval. Limit: identical variance can accompany very different shapes; squaring gives extremes substantial influence.
σ2=E⁡[(X−μ)2],μ=E⁡[X]m2=1n∑i(xi−xˉ)2=n−1ns2\begin{gathered}\sigma^2=\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^2],\quad\mu=\operatorname{E}[X]\\m_2=\frac1n\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2=\frac{n-1}{n}s^2\end{gathered}σ2=E[(X−μ)2],μ=E[X]m2​=n1​i∑​(xi​−xˉ)2=nn−1​s2​\begin{gathered}\sigma^2=\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^2],\quad\mu=\operatorname{E}[X]\\m_2=\frac1n\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2=\frac{n-1}{n}s^2\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für empirical central moment
X, μ, E[ ] and σ²
X: random measurement; μ: its expectation; E[ ]: population expectation; σ²: population variance. A finite second moment is required.
m₂ and s²
m₂: empirical variance with divisor n; s²: sample variance with n−1. Their relation requires n > 1. All variances have squared measurement units.
xᵢ, x̄, n, i and Σ
xᵢ: observed value i; x̄: sample mean; n: sample size; i: index 1 to n; Σ: sum over those observations. The empirical squared deviations concern this sample, not a known population σ².

59. Variance: identical squared spread does not identify shape

Variance: identical squared spread does not identify shape

60. Skewness: balance of signed cubic deviations

Skewness: balance of signed cubic deviations
Meaning Skewness standardizes the third central moment. Positive values mean stronger positive cubic contributions; negative values mean stronger negative contributions. It is dimensionless. Compare three shapes Uniform and normal-like: g₁ ≈ 0. Right-skewed: g₁ ≈ 1.759, with mean 50 above median 46.919 a.u. The next panels mark mean in cyan, median in dashed violet. Point size shows cubic-contribution magnitude; violet/orange distinguishes negative/positive deviations. The coefficient itself is printed, not placed on the measurement axis. Limit: zero skewness does not establish symmetry or a normal distribution.
γ1=E⁡[(X−μ)3]σ3,σ>0g1=m3m23/2,m2>0\begin{gathered}\gamma_1=\frac{\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^3]}{\sigma^3},\quad\sigma>0\\g_1=\frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}},\quad m_2>0\end{gathered}γ1​=σ3E[(X−μ)3]​,σ>0g1​=m23/2​m3​​,m2​>0​\begin{gathered}\gamma_1=\frac{\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^3]}{\sigma^3},\quad\sigma>0\\g_1=\frac{m_3}{m_2^{3/2}},\quad m_2>0\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für descriptive sample skewness
γ₁ and g₁
γ₁: population skewness; g₁: descriptive sample counterpart. Both are dimensionless; no small-sample bias adjustment is applied to g₁.
E[ ], X, μ and σ
E[ ]: population expectation; X: random measurement; μ: population mean; σ: population SD. A finite third absolute moment and σ > 0 are required.
m₃ and m₂
m₃: average cubed deviation from the sample mean; m₂: average squared deviation, each using n. Dividing by m₂^(3/2) removes the cubed unit. g₁ is undefined if m₂ = 0.

61. Skewness: distinguish positive and negative contributions

Skewness: distinguish positive and negative contributions

62. Kurtosis: weight of extreme standardized deviations

Kurtosis: weight of extreme standardized deviations
Meaning Kurtosis averages fourth powers of deviations after removing location and scale. It is dimensionless, not a horizontal coordinate or an interval. Compare three shapes Uniform K ≈ 1.800; normal-like 2.834; right-skewed 6.662. Excess kurtosis subtracts the normal-population benchmark 3. In the next point plots, larger points indicate larger fourth-power contributions. The cyan band is mean ± two divisor-n SDs, only a visual scale guide. Limit: kurtosis is not peak height, a mode count or a tail probability. A few extreme values can dominate; m₂ must be positive.
κ=E⁡[(X−μ)4]σ4,σ>0K=m4m22,g2=K−3,m2>0\begin{gathered}\kappa=\frac{\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^4]}{\sigma^4},\quad\sigma>0\\K=\frac{m_4}{m_2^2},\quad g_2=K-3,\quad m_2>0\end{gathered}κ=σ4E[(X−μ)4]​,σ>0K=m22​m4​​,g2​=K−3,m2​>0​\begin{gathered}\kappa=\frac{\operatorname{E}[(X-\mu)^4]}{\sigma^4},\quad\sigma>0\\K=\frac{m_4}{m_2^2},\quad g_2=K-3,\quad m_2>0\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für population kurtosis
κ, X, μ, σ and E[ ]
κ: population kurtosis; X: random measurement; μ: population mean; σ: population SD; E[ ]: expectation. A finite fourth moment and σ > 0 are required.
K, m₄ and m₂
K: descriptive sample kurtosis. m₄ and m₂ average fourth and squared deviations from the sample mean, using n. K is dimensionless and requires m₂ > 0.
g₂ and 3
g₂: sample excess K−3, without bias correction. Population excess: κ−3; 3 is normal-population kurtosis, not every normal sample's value.

63. Kurtosis: follow the extreme-deviation contributions

Kurtosis: follow the extreme-deviation contributions

64. Zero skewness does not imply symmetry

Zero skewness does not imply symmetry
Exact 50-residual counterexample 5 residuals equal −3, 25 equal −1, and 20 equal +2 a.u. Mean = (−15−25+40)/50 = 0. Calculate m₃ = [5(−27)+25(−1)+20(8)]/50 = 0; m₂ = 3; therefore g₁ = 0. But the sample is asymmetric: −3 has no matching +3 group; +2 has no matching −2 group. Signed cubes cancel without mirror symmetry. ==Inspect the distribution, not just the coefficient.==

65. R lab: moments, transformations and distribution checks

R lab: moments, transformations and distribution checks

Three synthetic shapes, **100 values each**. Rows compare shapes; columns show **points, boxplot, histogram**. - [!] **Run:** switch **metric**: mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis. - [!] **Change:** vary **offset**, **scale_factor**, then **extreme**, one at a time. - [?] **Explain:** what changes? Why does **m2** differ from **var(x)**? ==Geometric guides do not guarantee coverage.== Base R only. Local execution; no package download.

Three synthetic shapes, **100 values each**. Rows compare shapes; columns show **points, boxplot, histogram**. - [!] **Run:** switch **metric**: mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis. - [!] **Change:** vary **offset**, **scale_factor**, then **extreme**, one at a time. - [?] **Explain:** what changes? Why does **m2** differ from **var(x)**? ==Geometric guides do not guarantee coverage.== Base R only. Local execution; no package download.

# Deterministic synthetic grids; same construction as the lecture
p <- ((1:100) - 0.5) / 100
standardize <- function(z) 50 + 10 * as.numeric(scale(z))
series <- list(Uniform=standardize(p), Normal=standardize(qnorm(p)), Skewed=standardize(qexp(p)))
offset <- 0
scale_factor <- 1
extreme <- FALSE
metric <- 'variance'  # mean, variance, kurtosis, skewness
stopifnot(metric %in% c('mean','variance','kurtosis','skewness'))
series <- lapply(series, function(x) offset + scale_factor*x)
if (extreme) series$Normal[100] <- series$Normal[100] + 50

describe <- function(x) {
  d <- x-mean(x); m2 <- mean(d^2)
  c(mean=mean(x), m2=m2, sample_variance=var(x),
    kurtosis=if(m2>0) mean(d^4)/m2^2 else NA_real_,
    skewness=if(m2>0) mean(d^3)/m2^1.5 else NA_real_)
}
print(t(sapply(series, describe)))
x <- series$Normal; m2 <- mean((x-mean(x))^2)
cat('n =',length(x),'; sample variance =',var(x),'; m2 =',m2,'\n')

# Shared measurement axes and histogram edges
limits <- range(unlist(series)); if(diff(limits)==0) limits <- limits+c(-1,1)
edges <- seq(limits[1], limits[2], length.out=17)
mark <- function(x) {
  mu <- mean(x); root_m2 <- sqrt(mean((x-mu)^2))
  abline(v=mu,col='deepskyblue3',lwd=2)
  if(metric=='variance') abline(v=mu+c(-1,1)*root_m2,col='deepskyblue3',lty=3)
  if(metric=='kurtosis') abline(v=mu+c(-2,2)*root_m2,col='orange3',lty=3)
  if(metric=='skewness') abline(v=median(x),col='purple3',lty=2,lwd=2)
}
interpolated_box <- function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x,c(.25,.5,.75),type=7)
  width <- q[3]-q[1]
  inside <- x[x>=q[1]-1.5*width & x<=q[3]+1.5*width]
  flagged <- x[x<q[1]-1.5*width | x>q[3]+1.5*width]
  plot(NA,xlim=limits,ylim=c(0,1),yaxt='n',ylab='',
       main='Boxplot: linear interpolation',xlab='Response (a.u.)')
  segments(min(inside),.5,max(inside),.5)
  segments(c(min(inside),max(inside)),.4,c(min(inside),max(inside)),.6)
  rect(q[1],.3,q[3],.7,col='lavender',border='purple3')
  segments(q[2],.3,q[2],.7,lwd=2)
  points(flagged,rep(.5,length(flagged)),pch=16,cex=.5,col='orange3')
  mark(x)
  print(c(Q1=q[1],median=q[2],Q3=q[3],
          lower_whisker=min(inside),upper_whisker=max(inside)))
}
par(mfrow=c(3,3),mar=c(3,3,2.8,0.7),cex=0.7)
for(name in names(series)) {
  x <- series[[name]]; result <- describe(x)
  key <- if(metric=='variance') 'm2' else metric
  label <- paste(name,key,'=',round(result[key],3))
  stripchart(x,method='stack',pch=16,cex=0.45,xlim=limits,
             main=label,xlab='Response (a.u.)'); mark(x)
  interpolated_box(x)
  hist(x,breaks=edges,right=FALSE,include.lowest=TRUE,
       main='Histogram: common edges',xlab='Response (a.u.)'); mark(x)
}
cat('Variance guide: mean +/- sqrt(m2); kurtosis guide: mean +/- 2*sqrt(m2). Neither is a universal coverage interval.\n')
a <- rep(c(-3,-1,2),c(5,25,20))
cat('Counterexample: mean =',mean(a),'; m3 =',mean((a-mean(a))^3),'\n')
stopifnot(length(x)==100,isTRUE(all.equal(var(x),mean((x-mean(x))^2)*100/99)))

m2 <- mean(d^2) c(mean=mean(x), m2=m2, sample_variance=var(x), kurtosis=if(m2>0) mean(d^4)/m2^2 else NA_real_, skewness=if(m2>0) mean(d^3)/m2^1.5 else NA_real_) } print(t(sapply(series, describe))) x <- series$Normal; m2 <- mean((x-mean(x))^2) cat('n =',length(x),'; sample variance =',var(x),'; m2 =',m2,'\n') # Shared measurement axes and histogram edges limits <- range(unlist(series)); if(diff(limits)==0) limits <- limits+c(-1,1) edges <- seq(limits[1], limits[2], length.out=17) mark <- function(x) { mu <- mean(x); root_m2 <- sqrt(mean((x-mu)^2)) abline(v=mu,col='deepskyblue3',lwd=2) if(metric=='variance') abline(v=mu+c(-1,1)*root_m2,col='deepskyblue3',lty=3) if(metric=='kurtosis') abline(v=mu+c(-2,2)*root_m2,col='orange3',lty=3) if(metric=='skewness') abline(v=median(x),col='purple3',lty=2,lwd=2) } interpolated_box <- function(x) { q <- quantile(x,c(.25,.5,.75),type=7) width <- q[3]-q[1] inside <- x[x>=q[1]-1.5*width & x<=q[3]+1.5*width] flagged <- x[x<q[1]-1.5*width | x>q[3]+1.5*width] plot(NA,xlim=limits,ylim=c(0,1),yaxt='n',ylab='', main='Boxplot: linear interpolation',xlab='Response (a.u.)') segments(min(inside),.5,max(inside),.5) segments(c(min(inside),max(inside)),.4,c(min(inside),max(inside)),.6) rect(q[1],.3,q[3],.7,col='lavender',border='purple3') segments(q[2],.3,q[2],.7,lwd=2) points(flagged,rep(.5,length(flagged)),pch=16,cex=.5,col='orange3') mark(x) print(c(Q1=q[1],median=q[2],Q3=q[3], lower_whisker=min(inside),upper_whisker=max(inside))) } par(mfrow=c(3,3),mar=c(3,3,2.8,0.7),cex=0.7) for(name in names(series)) { x <- series[[name]]; mark(x) interpolated_box(x) hist(x,breaks=edges,right=FALSE,include.lowest=TRUE, main='Histogram: common edges',xlab='Response (a.u.)'); mark(x) } cat('Variance guide: mean +/- sqrt(m2); kurtosis guide: mean +/- 2*sqrt(m2). Neither is a universal coverage interval.\n') a <- rep(c(-3,-1,2),c(5,25,20)) cat('Counterexample: mean =',mean(a),'; m3 =',mean((a-mean(a))^3),'\n') stopifnot(length(x)==100,isTRUE(all.equal(var(x),mean((x-mean(x))^2)*100/99)))

standardize(z)
Local helper: rescale a synthetic grid to sample mean 50 and sample SD 10. Not a fitted population model.
scale(z)
By default subtract the mean and divide by sample SD. Returns a matrix with scaling attributes.
as.numeric(...)
Convert the scaled matrix to a plain numeric vector, dropping its matrix shape and attributes.
qnorm(p)
Return standard-normal quantiles at p. Here p is a deterministic midpoint grid, not random sampling.
qexp(p)
Return exponential quantiles (default rate 1), supplying the right-skewed grid before standardization.
c(...)
Combine values or named results into a vector; does not sort them.
list(...)
Collect the three named series, retaining each as a separate numeric vector.
lapply(series, function(x) ...)
Transform every series by the same offset/scale setting; return a list of transformed vectors.
sapply(series, describe)
Run describe() on each series; simplify equally sized result vectors into a matrix.
t(...)
Transpose the summary matrix so each printed row is one series.
describe(x)
Local helper: return mean, two variance conventions, skewness and Pearson kurtosis K, not excess. Constant data give undefined shape coefficients.
mean(x)
Calculate an arithmetic mean. Averaging powers of centred deviations gives empirical moments with divisor n.
var(x)
Calculate sample variance with divisor n−1, not descriptive variance with divisor n.
median(x)
Return the middle ordered value, averaging the two middle values for even n. Used for the dashed comparison line.
sqrt(...)
Take the nonnegative square root: convert descriptive variance into a spread guide in the original unit.
length(x)
Count vector elements, including ties. Each teaching series should contain 100 observations.
print(...)
Display computed result vectors or matrices explicitly in the text output.
cat(...)
Write labelled values and line breaks to the text output; does not return a table.
unlist(series)
Flatten the list only to find shared axis limits; series stay separate for analysis.
range(...)
Return the smallest and largest values across the series, defining shared measurement limits.
diff(limits)
Subtract consecutive values. For two limits this gives the axis width; zero triggers safe plotting expansion.
seq(..., length.out=17)
Generate 17 shared edges spanning the limits, giving 16 histogram bins in every row.
quantile(x, ..., type=7)
Compute quartiles by linear interpolation, not the alternative hinges of some boxplot implementations. The numeric argument selects this calculation in R.
min(inside), max(inside)
min() selects the smallest and max() the largest observation inside the fences. Those observations end the whiskers.
rep(...)
Repeat point heights or values. A vector of counts sets each value's multiplicity in the asymmetric counterexample.
par(mfrow=c(3,3), ...)
mfrow fills nine panels row by row; mar sets margins; cex sets text/symbol scaling.
names(series)
Return the series names for iteration and labels.
paste(...)
Combine series name, descriptor name and value into a plot title.
round(..., 3)
Round the displayed label to three decimals; calculations retain unrounded values.
stripchart(..., method="stack")
Draw individual observations with stacking. Point height is not time or a second measurement.
plot(NA, xlim=..., ylim=...)
Create an empty frame for the custom boxplot, with explicit shared limits and axis labels.
segments(...)
Draw line segments for whiskers, end caps and the median.
rect(...)
Draw the box between the explicitly calculated first and third quartiles.
points(...)
Add orange points for observations outside the fences; they remain in the sample.
abline(v=..., col=..., lty=..., lwd=...)
Add vertical reference lines: v position, col colour, lty dash style, lwd width. No probability is estimated.
hist(..., breaks=edges, right=FALSE, include.lowest=TRUE)
Use shared explicit bins. right=FALSE makes them left-closed; include.lowest=TRUE includes the terminal endpoint for this closure.
mark(x)
Local helper: draw the mean and metric-specific guides. metric selects the guide, not a new dataset or confidence interval.
interpolated_box(x)
Local helper: draw linearly interpolated quartiles, observed whiskers and flagged points; print their numerical boundaries.
stopifnot(...)
Stop if a check fails. The metric check limits allowed settings; the final check inspects the last loop series, not all three.
isTRUE(all.equal(...))
all.equal() compares with numerical tolerance, returning TRUE or a diagnostic; isTRUE() produces one logical pass/fail value.
function, for, if / else, <-, $, [, [[, %in% and arithmetic
function defines helpers; for repeats; if/else branches. <- assigns; $, [, [[ select data; %in% tests membership. : makes integer sequences; + − * / calculate; ^ raises powers. Comparisons return logical values; & / | combine them. NA_real_ marks undefined numeric coefficients.

Topic: Distribution functions

1. Start with the random quantity, then choose its model

Start with the random quantity, then choose its model
Why do measurements vary?
Observe repeated results and define the random quantity.
Why a bell-shaped model?
Combine suitable independent additive effects.
Why a long right tail?
Model relative effects on the log scale.
How random is estimated spread?
Study sample variances and standardized means.
How can we compare methods?
Describe variance ratios with the F distribution.
How do we check our models?
Compare data with model quantiles, CDFs and expected counts.

Topic: Distribution functions

2. Which questions can a probability distribution answer?

Which questions can a probability distribution answer?
How often in a range?
Choose a concentration interval. Its probability is the area under the model density.
How much is below a limit?
The cumulative distribution gives the probability at or below a threshold.
Which limit gives a chosen probability?
Choose a cumulative probability. The quantile gives its corresponding threshold.

Topic: Distribution functions

3. One unchanged sample can produce different results

One unchanged sample can produce different results
A measurement model connects the reported result with the contributions of injection, flow, temperature and electronics. Repetition under the same conditions reveals their combined variation.

Topic: Distribution functions

4. More results reveal the assumed distribution more clearly

More results reveal the assumed distribution more clearly
A larger simulated sample reveals the generating distribution more clearly while the method's population spread stays unchanged.
# Assumed normal generator, not fitted or measured validation data.
M <- 20 # Try 20, 50, 100, 1000. The browser uses these saved prefixes.
stopifnot(M %in% c(20,50,100,1000))
state <- 20261102; x <- numeric(M)
for(i in seq_len(M)) {
  state <- (16807 * state) %% 2147483647
  x[i] <- 10 + .10 * qnorm(state/2147483647)
}
edges <- seq(9.60,10.40,by=.05)
h <- hist(x,breaks=edges,right=FALSE,plot=FALSE)
cat('M:',M,'counted:',sum(h$counts),'\n')
cat('Counts:',h$counts,'\n')
plot(h,freq=FALSE,col='#8ecae6',xlab='Nitrate result (mg/L)',
     ylab='Simulated density (L/mg)',main='Assumed stable normal generator')

# Assumed normal generator, not fitted or measured validation data. M <- 20 # Try 20, 50, 100, 1000. The browser uses these saved prefixes. stopifnot(M %in% c(20,50,100,1000)) state <- 20261102; x <- numeric(M) for(i in seq_len(M)) { state <- (16807 * state) %% 2147483647 x[i] <- 10 + .10 * qnorm(state/2147483647) } edges <- seq(9.60,10.40,by=.05) h <- hist(x,breaks=edges,right=FALSE,plot=FALSE) cat('M:',M,'counted:',sum(h$counts),'\n') cat('Counts:',h$counts,'\n') plot(h,freq=FALSE,col='#8ecae6',xlab='Nitrate result (mg/L)', ylab='Simulated density (L/mg)',main='Assumed stable normal generator')

R functions and the deterministic stream
- Choose the sample size. c lists the allowed result counts. %in% checks whether M belongs to that list, and stopifnot enforces this choice. - Prepare the simulation. numeric allocates the result vector; seq_len supplies the iteration indices. - Generate reproducible results. The Park–Miller recurrence updates an integer-valued state using multiplication and the remainder operator %%. qnorm transforms the resulting uniform fractions into standard-normal values. Scaling and shifting set the stated SD and mean. - Build the histogram. seq creates fixed bin edges. hist computes and draws density bins whose left edges belong to the bin. - Check the counts. sum totals the bin counts; cat reports that total alongside M so that count conservation can be checked.

5. Area under the density gives interval probability

Area under the density gives interval probability
P(a≤X≤b)=∫abf(x) dx=F(b)−F(a)P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)P(a≤X≤b)=∫ab​f(x)dx=F(b)−F(a)P(a\le X\le b)=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)Mathematische Formel für Probability density function
interval probability and density area
X
Random individual nitrate concentration (mg/L).
x
Concrete concentration coordinate (mg/L).
a, b
Ordered lower and upper interval bounds (mg/L).
P
Probability of the stated event (dimensionless).
f(x)
Model probability density at x (L/mg).
F(x)
Cumulative probability at or below x (dimensionless).
∫, dx
Accumulate density over the interval; dx is an infinitesimal concentration increment (mg/L).
≤
Includes the interval endpoints, each with zero point probability.
=, −
Equality between equivalent probabilities; subtraction of the lower CDF value from the upper.

The density is nonnegative and has total area one. Integrating density times concentration gives a dimensionless probability.

6. A quantile turns probability into a threshold

A quantile turns probability into a threshold
F(x)=P(X≤x)=∫−∞xf(t) dtf(x)=F′(x)where the derivative existsxp=F−1(p)\begin{gathered}F(x)=P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt\\f(x)=F'(x)\quad\text{where the derivative exists}\\x_p=F^{-1}(p)\end{gathered}F(x)=P(X≤x)=∫−∞x​f(t)dtf(x)=F′(x)where the derivative existsxp​=F−1(p)​\begin{gathered}F(x)=P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)\,dt\\f(x)=F'(x)\quad\text{where the derivative exists}\\x_p=F^{-1}(p)\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für Cumulative distribution function
general PDF and CDF
X
Random concentration (mg/L).
x
Concrete concentration threshold (mg/L).
F(x)

P, ≤
Probability of an event; at or below the threshold.
f(t)

t, dt

∫, −∞
Integrate up to x over an unbounded lower range.
F′(x)
Derivative of F with respect to x; the local slope (L/mg).
=

Conditions: the integral representation uses an absolutely continuous model. The slope equals f where the derivative relation holds. Every distribution has a CDF; existence of a PDF requires additional conditions.

quantile as the reversed cumulative question

xpx_pxp​

The generalized inverse is the greatest lower bound of thresholds whose cumulative probability is at least ppp. For continuous, strictly increasing FFF, it is the usual inverse function. In these continuous examples, p=0.95p = 0.95p=0.95 places 95% probability at or below xpx_pxp​.

Answer: the model's 0.95 quantile (95% reference example; controls explore other probabilities).

The same concentration gap can mean different tail probabilities

Method-identifying subscripts.
−, /, =

10. Φ\PhiΦ gives cumulative standard-Normal probability

Φ\PhiΦ gives cumulative standard-Normal probability
Φ(z)=P(Z≤z)=∫−∞zφ(t) dt=12[1+erf⁡ ⁣(z2)]erf⁡(u)=2π∫0ue−t2 dtΦ(2)≈0.9772499\begin{gathered}\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\\=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\varphi(t)\,dt\\=\frac12\left[1+\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt2}\right)\right]\\\operatorname{erf}(u)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^u e^{-t^2}\,dt\\\Phi(2)\approx0.9772499\end{gathered}Φ(z)=P(Z≤z)=∫−∞z​φ(t)dt=21​[1+erf(2​z​)]erf(u)=π​2​∫0u​e−t2dtΦ(2)≈0.9772499​\begin{gathered}\Phi(z)=P(Z\le z)\\=\int_{-\infty}^{z}\varphi(t)\,dt\\=\frac12\left[1+\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt2}\right)\right]\\\operatorname{erf}(u)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\int_0^u e^{-t^2}\,dt\\\Phi(2)\approx0.9772499\end{gathered}The normal density has no elementary antiderivative. Its CDF is an antiderivative expressed using the special error function erf. Scaling the argument by the square root of two and applying the half-offset gives the standard-normal CDF, with its integration constant fixed by probability zero at minus infinity. The error function itself is not the normal CDF and is not a probability.
accumulated left-tail probability
Φ(z)
Standard-normal cumulative probability at z; a special case of F.
φ(t)

Z
Standard-normal random variable.
z
Concrete standardized threshold, 2 here (dimensionless).
t
Dimensionless integration variable.
P, ≤
Probability; at or below the threshold.
∫, −∞, dt
Integrate from minus infinity up to z; dt is the increment of t.
=, ≈
Equality and approximate equality.

The CDF slope equals the density where the derivative exists. All quantities use the standardized, dimensionless scale.

error function
erf(u)
Error function at dimensionless argument u.
u
Upper integration limit in the definition of erf.
t, dt
Dimensionless integration variable and its infinitesimal increment.
∫₀ᵘ
Integrate from zero to u.
e⁻ᵗ²
Natural exponential with exponent −t².
π

Positive square root.
2 / √π

z / √2

½, 1, +
Multiply the grouped expression by one half after adding one.
( ), [ ]
Group the stated operations.

All quantities here are dimensionless. The error function erf provides the special-function representation of the standard-normal density's antiderivative. Integrating from minus infinity fixes the CDF normalization.

11. A fixed limit's exceedance probability depends on model spread

φ(2)≈0.05399P(X>10.20)=1−Φ(2)≈0.02275\begin{gathered}\varphi(2)\approx0.05399\\P(X>10.20)=1-\Phi(2)\\\approx0.02275\end{gathered}φ(2)≈0.05399P(X>10.20)=1−Φ(2)≈0.02275​\begin{gathered}\varphi(2)\approx0.05399\\P(X>10.20)=1-\Phi(2)\\\approx0.02275\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für Normal model for repeated measurements

X
Normal random concentration (mg/L), with mean 10.00 mg/L and SD 0.10 mg/L.
z

# Fixed known model. Change limit, mu or sigma; no parameter estimation.
mu <- 10.00; sigma <- 0.10; limit <- 10.20; alpha <- 0.01
stopifnot(is.finite(mu),is.finite(limit),is.finite(sigma),sigma>0,
          alpha>0,alpha<1)
z <- (limit-mu)/sigma
phi <- dnorm(z); Phi <- pnorm(z)
upper <- pnorm(z,lower.tail=FALSE)
eta_star <- qnorm(1-alpha); x_star <- mu+sigma*eta_star
cat('z-score:',z,'\n')
cat('phi: density per z-unit, NOT a probability:',phi,'\n')
cat('Phi: probability at or below limit:',Phi,'\n')
cat('Above limit:',100*upper,'%\n')
cat('Upper',100*alpha,'% threshold (mg/L):',format(x_star,digits=12),'\n')
old <- par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(5,4,3,1))
grid <- seq(-4,4,length.out=801)
plot(grid,dnorm(grid),type='l',col='#176b90',lwd=2,
     xlab='Standardized threshold z',ylab='Density per z-unit',main='Lowercase phi')
cut <- max(-4,min(4,z)); left <- seq(-4,cut,length.out=400)
polygon(c(-4,left,cut),c(0,dnorm(left),0),col='#8ecae6',border=NA)
abline(v=z,col='#a63d21',lty=2)
plot(grid,pnorm(grid),type='l',col='#176b90',lwd=2,ylim=c(0,1),
     xlab='Standardized threshold z',ylab='Cumulative probability',main='Uppercase Phi')
abline(v=z,h=Phi,col='#a63d21',lty=2)
par(old)
cat('Graphs show z -4 to 4; probabilities use the full normal law.\n')

12. The ECDF accumulates observed sample fractions

The ECDF accumulates observed sample fractions
# Same deterministic 1000-draw sample as the saved histogram.
M <- 1000; mu <- 10.00; sigma <- 0.10; state <- 20261102
x <- numeric(M)
for(i in seq_len(M)) {
  state <- (16807*state) %% 2147483647
  x[i] <- mu+sigma*qnorm(state/2147483647)
}
Fn <- ecdf(x)
cat('Observed fractions at 9.80, 10.00, 10.20:',Fn(c(9.8,10,10.2)),'\n')
cat('Theoretical CDF at 10.20:',pnorm(10.2,mu,sigma),'\n')
cat('Observed upper fraction:',mean(x>10.2),'\n')
plot(Fn,verticals=FALSE,do.points=FALSE,col='#176b90',lwd=2,
     main='1000 observations versus an assumed model',
     xlab='Nitrate threshold (mg/L)',ylab='Cumulative probability')
curve(pnorm(x,mean=mu,sd=sigma),add=TRUE,col='#a63d21',lwd=2)
legend('topleft',c('Empirical step CDF','Fixed theoretical CDF'),
       col=c('#176b90','#a63d21'),lty=1,bty='n')
