Topic: Continuous models · Lognormal

15. Multiplicative factors motivate a different model

Multiplicative factors motivate a different model
A: repeat the instrument step
Organic trace analyte by LC-MS/MS, in ng/L. Reinject one prepared homogeneous control. The simplified instrument model uses mainly additive error.
B: repeat the complete preparation
Independently extract, concentrate and analyse aliquots from one homogeneous sample. Relative step-to-step effects motivate a multiplicative candidate model.

Topic: Continuous models · Lognormal

16. Positive relative factors can produce a long right tail

Positive relative factors can produce a long right tail
# Separate fictional series, not paired validation measurements.
# Relative factors are NOT literal unbounded extraction recoveries.
M <- 1000; steps <- 3; factor_model <- 'normal'
x0 <- 10; sd_instrument <- 0.10; sigma_L <- 0.30; state <- 20261103
stopifnot(M>=10,M<=10000,steps>=1,steps<=200,
          factor_model %in% c('normal','binary'))
A <- numeric(M); B <- numeric(M); log_total <- numeric(M)
for(j in seq_len(M)) {
  state <- (16807*state) %% 2147483647
  A[j] <- x0+sd_instrument*qnorm(state/2147483647)
  contributions <- numeric(steps)
  for(i in seq_len(steps)) {
    state <- (16807*state) %% 2147483647
    u <- state/2147483647
    contributions[i] <- sigma_L/sqrt(steps) *
      if(factor_model=='normal') qnorm(u) else if(u<0.5) -1 else 1
  }
  log_total[j] <- sum(contributions)
  B[j] <- x0*prod(exp(contributions))
}
cat('Instrument mean and SD (ng/L):',mean(A),sd(A),'\n')
cat('Preparation mean (ng/L):',mean(B),'log SD:',sd(log_total),'\n')
cat('Preparation count above 15 ng/L:',sum(B>15),'of',M,'\n')
edges_B <- seq(0,max(36,ceiling(max(B)/2)*2),by=2)
hB <- hist(B,breaks=edges_B,right=FALSE,plot=FALSE)
cat('Preparation bin counts:',hB$counts,'\n')
cat('Normal log factors: exact lognormal. Binary log factors: finite discrete model.\n')
old <- par(mfrow=c(1,2),mar=c(5,4,3,1))
hist(A,breaks=seq(floor(min(A)/.05)*.05,ceiling(max(A)/.05)*.05,by=.05),
     right=FALSE,probability=TRUE,col='#8ecae6',main='A: instrument only',
     xlab='Result (ng/L)',ylab='Density (L/ng)')
plot(hB,freq=FALSE,col='#8ecae6',main='B: complete preparation',
     xlab='Result (ng/L)',ylab='Density (L/ng)')
par(old)
cat('Panel ranges differ; the concentration units are the same.\n')

18. Exponentiating a normal log ratio creates the model

Exponentiating a normal log ratio creates the model
Y=ln⁡(X/xref)∼N(μL,σL2)X=xrefeY\begin{gathered}Y=\ln(X/x_{\mathrm{ref}})\sim\mathcal N(\mu_L,\sigma_L^2)\\X=x_{\mathrm{ref}}e^Y\end{gathered}Y=ln(X/xref​)∼N(μL​,σL2​)X=xref​eY​\begin{gathered}Y=\ln(X/x_{\mathrm{ref}})\sim\mathcal N(\mu_L,\sigma_L^2)\\X=x_{\mathrm{ref}}e^Y\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für Lognormal concentration model
the transformed normal model
X
Positive random concentration (ng/L).
xrefx_{ref}xref​
Fixed positive reference concentration, 10 ng/L; subscript ref means reference.
YYY
Natural log ratio ln⁡(X/xref)\ln(X / x_{ref})ln(X/xref​), dimensionless.
μLμ_LμL​
Mean of the log ratio, dimensionless; subscript L identifies the log scale.
σLσ_LσL​
Positive SD of the log ratio, dimensionless.
N,∼N, ∼N,∼
Normal distribution; follows that distribution. Its second parameter is variance σL2σ_L^2σL2​.
ln, e
Natural logarithm and the base of the natural exponential.
/, ², =
Division, squaring and equality defining the transforms.

Here μL=0μ_L = 0μL​=0 and σL=0.30σ_L = 0.30σL​=0.30, giving median 10 ng/L. Multiplying the exponentiated ratio by the reference restores concentration units.

# Fixed median 10 ng/L; log SD changes, not the reference units.
M <- 10000; x_ref <- 10; mu_L <- 0; sigma_L <- 0.30; state <- 20261103
stopifnot(M>=100,M<=10000,x_ref>0,sigma_L>0,sigma_L<=1)
Y <- numeric(M)
for(i in seq_len(M)) {
  state <- (16807*state) %% 2147483647
  Y[i] <- mu_L+sigma_L*qnorm(state/2147483647)
}
X <- x_ref*exp(Y)
model_mode <- x_ref*exp(mu_L-sigma_L^2)
model_median <- x_ref*exp(mu_L)
model_mean <- x_ref*exp(mu_L+sigma_L^2/2)
cat('Population mode, median, mean (ng/L):',model_mode,model_median,model_mean,'\n')
cat('Sample geometric mean (ng/L):',x_ref*exp(mean(log(X/x_ref))),'\n')
cat('Upper probability above 15 ng/L:',pnorm((log(15/x_ref)-mu_L)/sigma_L,lower.tail=FALSE),'\n')
q95 <- x_ref*exp(mu_L+sigma_L*qnorm(.95))
cat('Population 95th percentile (ng/L):',format(q95,digits=12),'\n')
old <- par(mfrow=c(1,3),mar=c(5,4,3,1))
hist(Y,probability=TRUE,col='#8ecae6',main='Normal log ratios',
     xlab='Y: natural log ratio',ylab='Density per log-ratio unit')
curve(dnorm(x,mu_L,sigma_L),add=TRUE,col='#a63d21',lwd=2)
hist(X,probability=TRUE,col='#8ecae6',main='Exponentiated results',
     xlab='Concentration (ng/L)',ylab='Density (L/ng)')
curve(dlnorm(x/x_ref,meanlog=mu_L,sdlog=sigma_L)/x_ref,
      add=TRUE,col='#a63d21',lwd=2)
grid <- seq(.01,35,length.out=1000)
spreads <- c(.15,.30,.60); colors <- c('#176b90','#a63d21','#5c469c')
densities <- sapply(spreads,function(s) dlnorm(grid/x_ref,mu_L,s)/x_ref)
matplot(grid,densities,type='l',lty=1,col=colors,lwd=2,
        xlab='Concentration (ng/L)',ylab='Density (L/ng)',main='Same median, different log SD')
legend('topright',legend=spreads,col=colors,lty=1,bty='n',title='Log SD')
par(old)
cat('The comparison-density window ends at 35; tails and moments are not truncated.\n')

Topic: Continuous models · Lognormal

20. Match the lognormal model to the measurement process

Match the lognormal model to the measurement process
Mixtures: define the population
- Multiple sources: pooling can create skewness or several peaks. - ==Assess the model for the defined sampling population.== - Before fitting: identify the sampling population.
Censoring: respect the reporting limit
- ==A non-detect locates the result below a reporting threshold.== - Replacing all low results by one value: creates an artificial pile-up. - Model explicitly: observation process and reporting threshold.
Sites: environmental variation
- Different sites: genuine environmental variation and possible spatial dependence. - ==Define the population of sites and sampling conditions.== - Reporting target: arithmetic expectation and a typical log-scale center answer different questions.
# New population: between-site concentrations, NOT technical repeats.
M <- 100; mode <- 'candidate'; x_ref <- 10; sigma_site <- 0.60
loq <- 5; state <- 20261103
stopifnot(mode %in% c('candidate','mixture','censored'))
log_ratio <- numeric(M)
for(i in seq_len(M)) {
  state <- (16807*state) %% 2147483647
  log_ratio[i] <- sigma_site*qnorm(state/2147483647)
}
if(mode=='mixture') {
  for(i in seq_len(M)) {
    state <- (16807*state) %% 2147483647
    if(state/2147483647<.30) log_ratio[i] <- log_ratio[i]+1.2
  }
}
latent <- x_ref*exp(log_ratio)
observed <- latent
if(mode=='censored') observed[latent<loq] <- NA_real_
cat('Mode:',mode,'sites:',M,'censored:',sum(is.na(observed)),'\n')
if(mode=='censored') cat('Plots show detections only: selection-biased, NOT model validation.\n')
kept <- observed[!is.na(observed)]
stopifnot(all(kept>0))
logged <- log(kept/x_ref)
old <- par(mfrow=c(1,3),mar=c(5,4,3,1))
hist(kept,probability=TRUE,col='#8ecae6',main=paste(mode,'sites'),
     xlab='Concentration (ng/L)',ylab='Observed density (L/ng)')
hist(logged,probability=TRUE,col='#8ecae6',main='Same retained values, log ratios',
     xlab='Natural log ratio',ylab='Density per log-ratio unit')
qqnorm(logged,pch=16,cex=.6,col='#176b90',main='Normal Q-Q of log ratios')
qqline(logged,col='#a63d21',lwd=2)
par(old)
cat('A Q-Q plot does not establish independence. No zero substitution or log(0).\n')

24. An unchanged method still produces varying variance estimates

An unchanged method still produces varying variance estimates
# Hypothetical stable method. No field or validation data.
# First change M: 100, 1000, 10000. Later change n: 6, 30.
M <- 100; n <- 6; sigma <- 0.10; mu <- 10
stopifnot(M %in% c(100, 1000, 10000), n >= 2, n <= 100,
          n == as.integer(n), sigma > 0)
state <- 20261101
S2 <- numeric(M)
first <- numeric(n)
for (j in seq_len(M)) {
  x <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    state <- (16807 * state) %% 2147483647
    x[i] <- mu + sigma * qnorm(state / 2147483647)
  }
  if (j == 1) first <- x
  S2[j] <- sum((x - mean(x))^2) / (n - 1)
}
cat('First series (mg/L):', format(first, digits=8), '\n')
cat('M:', M, 'n:', n, 'df:', n-1, '\n')
cat('Mean sample variance:', mean(S2), '(mg/L)^2\n')
cat('Relative SD, empirical:', sd(S2)/mean(S2),
    'theoretical:', sqrt(2/(n-1)), '\n')
cat('Count at least observed variance 0.024:', sum(S2 >= 0.024), '\n')
old <- par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(5,4,3,1))
plot(seq_len(M), S2, pch=16, cex=0.35, col='#176b90',
     xlab='Independent series number', ylab='Sample variance ((mg/L)^2)',
     main=paste(M, 'complete series'), ylim=c(0,max(0.064,S2)))
abline(h=sigma^2, col='#a63d21', lty=2)
breaks <- seq(0, max(0.064, ceiling(max(S2)/0.002)*0.002), by=0.002)
hist(S2, breaks=breaks, right=FALSE, probability=TRUE, col='#8ecae6',
     xlab='Sample variance ((mg/L)^2)', ylab='Density per (mg/L)^2',
     main=paste('n =', n), xlim=c(0,max(breaks)))
abline(v=0.024, col='#a63d21', lwd=2)
par(old)

27. Scaled squared deviations make sample spread comparable

Scaled squared deviations make sample spread comparable
Put the observed spread on the reference scale
Scaling by an independently known reference SD makes squared residuals comparable across concentration units. Estimating one mean links the residuals and leaves five independent degrees of freedom in a six-result sample.
q=∑i=16(xi−xˉσ0)2=0.120.102=12q=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\left(\frac{x_i-\bar x}{\sigma_0}\right)^2=\frac{0.12}{0.10^2}=12q=i=1∑6​(σ0​xi​−xˉ​)2=0.1020.12​=12q=\sum_{i=1}^{6}\left(\frac{x_i-\bar x}{\sigma_0}\right)^2=\frac{0.12}{0.10^2}=12Mathematische Formel für Chi-square distribution
observed statistic
q
Observed statistic for this series (dimensionless).
xᵢ
IC measurement result i (mg/L).
x̄
Sample mean, 10.05 mg/L; the bar denotes averaging.
σ₀
Independently known reference SD, 0.10 mg/L; subscript 0 labels the reference.
squared scaled residuals
Σ
Add all six indexed terms.
i
Measurement index, from 1 through 6.
−
Subtract the sample mean from a measurement.
/, ²
Divide by the reference SD, then square the ratio.
=
Rewrites the same calculation; parentheses group each ratio.

The squared-deviation sum is 0.12 (mg/L)². Dividing by (0.10 mg/L)² cancels the units and gives q = 12.

28. An upper-tail comparison checks the reference precision

An upper-tail comparison checks the reference precision
Is this spread unusual under unchanged precision
Q = 12 exceeds the 5% cutoff 11.07; its boundary-model upper tail is 3.48%. This indicates increased spread under the stated assumptions. Investigating the analytical system is a separate step.
H0:σ≤σ0,H1:σ>σ0q=12>χ5;0.952≈11.07p=Pσ=σ0(Q≥12)≈0.03479\begin{gathered}H_0:\sigma\le\sigma_0,\quad H_1:\sigma>\sigma_0\\q=12>\chi^2_{5;0.95}\approx11.07\\p=P_{\sigma=\sigma_0}(Q\ge12)\approx0.03479\end{gathered}H0​:σ≤σ0​,H1​:σ>σ0​q=12>χ5;0.952​≈11.07p=Pσ=σ0​​(Q≥12)≈0.03479​\begin{gathered}H_0:\sigma\le\sigma_0,\quad H_1:\sigma>\sigma_0\\q=12>\chi^2_{5;0.95}\approx11.07\\p=P_{\sigma=\sigma_0}(Q\ge12)\approx0.03479\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für Chi-square distribution
decision notation
:
Introduces the statement of a hypothesis.
≤, >, ≥
At most, greater than and at least.
=, ≈
Equality and approximate equality.
α
Prespecified significance level, 0.05.

For σ below σ₀, the upper-tail rejection probability is smaller. Calibration at σ = σ₀ therefore controls the composite null.

H₁

σ₀

The comparison concerns repeatability spread.

Q

95th percentile of chi-square with five degrees of freedom.

Probability under the null boundary σ = σ₀.
p

All these quantities are dimensionless. The p-value is a probability about the statistic under the stated model.

# Hypothetical stable method. No field or validation data.
# First change M: 100, 1000, 10000. Later change n: 6, 30.
M <- 100; n <- 6; sigma <- 0.10; mu <- 10
stopifnot(M %in% c(100, 1000, 10000), n >= 2, n <= 100,
          n == as.integer(n), sigma > 0)
state <- 20261101
S2 <- numeric(M)
first <- numeric(n)
for (j in seq_len(M)) {
  x <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    state <- (16807 * state) %% 2147483647
    x[i] <- mu + sigma * qnorm(state / 2147483647)
  }
  if (j == 1) first <- x
  S2[j] <- sum((x - mean(x))^2) / (n - 1)
}
cat('First series (mg/L):', format(first, digits=8), '\n')
cat('M:', M, 'n:', n, 'df:', n-1, '\n')
cat('Mean sample variance:', mean(S2), '(mg/L)^2\n')
cat('Relative SD, empirical:', sd(S2)/mean(S2),
    'theoretical:', sqrt(2/(n-1)), '\n')
cat('Count at least observed variance 0.024:', sum(S2 >= 0.024), '\n')
old <- par(mfrow=c(1,2), mar=c(5,4,3,1))
plot(seq_len(M), S2, pch=16, cex=0.35, col='#176b90',
     xlab='Independent series number', ylab='Sample variance ((mg/L)^2)',
     main=paste(M, 'complete series'), ylim=c(0,max(0.064,S2)))
abline(h=sigma^2, col='#a63d21', lty=2)
breaks <- seq(0, max(0.064, ceiling(max(S2)/0.002)*0.002), by=0.002)
hist(S2, breaks=breaks, right=FALSE, probability=TRUE, col='#8ecae6',
     xlab='Sample variance ((mg/L)^2)', ylab='Density per (mg/L)^2',
     main=paste('n =', n), xlim=c(0,max(breaks)))
abline(v=0.024, col='#a63d21', lwd=2)
par(old)

Topic: Sampling · Student-t

31. An estimated denominator gives t its heavier tails

An estimated denominator gives t its heavier tails
Small denominator, large statistic
- Small estimated SE can magnify either sign of mean departure. - True generating SD stays fixed.
Heavier tails from an estimated standard error
- Symmetric t density: lower peak, heavier tails than normal. - Each complete sample contributes one studentized mean. - Normal sampling makes mean and variance independent.

Topic: Sampling · Student-t

32. More degrees of freedom bring t closer to Normal

More degrees of freedom bring t closer to Normal
- More measurements: a more stable estimated denominator. - More degrees of freedom: lighter tails, closer to the normal density. - Same center: the distributions remain symmetric around zero.

Topic: Connections · Distribution families

37. Each distribution family has a characteristic construction

Each distribution family has a characteristic construction
Normal: additive contributions
- Independent normal contributions: exact. - Many small effects: approximation under suitable conditions.
Y=X1+X2+X3+⋯Y=X_1+X_2+X_3+\cdotsY=X1​+X2​+X3​+⋯Y=X_1+X_2+X_3+\cdotsMathematische Formel für Distributions in analytical measurement

Y
Random total concentration contribution (mg/L).
X₁, X₂, X₃
Random additive contributions, such as injection, flow and detector effects (mg/L).
1, 2, 3
Subscripts identifying the contributions.
+
Addition.
…, =
Continuation of the finite sum; equality defining Y.

Independent Normal contributions give an exact Normal sum. A central-limit approximation requires suitable conditions, including finite variances and control of the individual contributions relative to the total variation.

Lognormal: relative factors
- Multiply positive relative factors. - A normal log-sum gives a lognormal product.
Y=X1⋅X2⋅X3⋯Y=X_1\cdot X_2\cdot X_3\cdotsY=X1​⋅X2​⋅X3​⋯Y=X_1\cdot X_2\cdot X_3\cdotsMathematische Formel für Distributions in analytical measurement

X₁, X₂, X₃
Positive random relative factors (dimensionless); subscripts identify the factors.
·
Multiplication of factors.
…, =
Continuation of the finite product; equality defining Y.

Condition: the sum of natural-log factors is Normal; independent Normal log factors suffice. Multiplying Y by a fixed reference concentration restores concentration units.

Chi-square: squared and scaled
- Add independent squared standard normals. - Normal samples: scaled sample variance.
Q=Z12+⋯+Zν2Q=(n−1)S2σ2\begin{gathered}Q=Z_1^2+\cdots+Z_\nu^2\\Q=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\end{gathered}Q=Z12​+⋯+Zν2​Q=σ2(n−1)S2​​\begin{gathered}Q=Z_1^2+\cdots+Z_\nu^2\\Q=\frac{(n-1)S^2}{\sigma^2}\end{gathered}Mathematische Formel für Distributions in analytical measurement

For sample variance, ν = n − 1. Scaling cancels concentration units. Independent Z components correspond to orthonormal residual coordinates; the raw centred residuals share the fitted mean.

Student-t: standardized means
- Center the mean; use its estimated standard error. - Independent normal measurements.

Estimated standard error of the mean (mg/L); the square root is positive.

Condition: independent, identically distributed Normal measurements. Sample variance uses divisor n − 1, giving n − 1 Student degrees of freedom.

- Two independent normal samples. - Normalize each variance by its true variance, then divide.

38. Q-Q plots compare observed and theoretical quantiles

Q-Q plots compare observed and theoretical quantiles
Read the pattern before calculating a test
Comparison with a fixed model assesses location, scale and shape together. Fitting a straight line adjusts location and scale to inspect shape. Five observations provide limited evidence about a population distribution.

Topic: Model checking · Q-Q, KS and Pearson

39. KS checks the largest ECDF–model gap, including jump sides

KS checks the largest ECDF–model gap, including jump sides
Fixed model: compare both distances with 0.563275
Fixed Normal model: mean 10 mg/L, SD 0.50 mg/L. For five independent continuous observations, the exact two-sided 5% cutoff is 0.563275. A: 0.144578 lies below it. B: 0.725747 exceeds it. Measure gaps on both sides of each ECDF jump.
A model fitted to these data needs another reference
Estimating mean and SD from the same observations changes the reference distribution. Use a suitable Lilliefors calibration or a parametric bootstrap that refits every replicate. Ties, censoring and dependence also need a matching calibration.
n <- 5; a <- 0.05  # sample size; upper-tail level
tail <- function(d) { k <- 0:floor(n*(1-d))
  2*d*sum(choose(n,k)*(d+k/n)^(k-1)*(1-d-k/n)^(n-k)) }
uniroot(function(d) tail(d)-a, c(.500001,.999999), tol=1e-12)$root
# 0.5632751984. Exact shortcut here requires d above 0.5.
